docs.title: Non-Affine Networks
docs.text:
For networks which contain both affine and non-affine elements, we can combine the characteristics of the affine elements as before and combine the characteristics of the non-affine elements into \(f_{\text{non-affine}} (\boldsymbol{v}, \boldsymbol{i}) = \boldsymbol{0}\).

We can then construct a tableau system of the following form:

\[ \left\vert \begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} \boldsymbol{B} & \boldsymbol{0} \\ \boldsymbol{0} & \boldsymbol{A} \\ \boldsymbol{M}' & \boldsymbol{N}' \end{bmatrix} \begin {bmatrix}\boldsymbol{v} \\ \boldsymbol{i}\end{bmatrix} & = \begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0} \\ \boldsymbol{0} \\ \boldsymbol{e}'\end{bmatrix} \\ f_{\text{non-affine}} (\boldsymbol{v}, \boldsymbol{i}) & = \boldsymbol{0} \end{aligned}\right. \]

docs.title: Capacitive One-Ports
docs.text:
Theorem: Work and Charge-Controlled Capacitive One-Ports

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a time-invariant capacitive one-port.

If \(\mathcal{C}\) has a charge-controlled representation \(v = \chi(q)\), then the work needed to change its charge from \(Q_{\text{initial}}\) to \(Q_{\text{final}}\) is given by the following integral:

\[W = \int_{Q_{\text{initial}}}^{Q_{\text{final}}} \chi(q) \, \mathrm{d}q\] Proof

docs.title: One-Ports in Parallel
docs.text:
Definition: One-Ports in Parallel

A parallel circuit is an electrical element which consists of one-ports whose terminals are connected at the same nodes.

We also say that the one-ports are connected in parallel.

Theorem: Voltage across Parallel Circuits

The voltage across all one-ports in a parallel circuit is the same.

Proof

TODO

Theorem: Equivalence of Parallel Circuits

Every parallel circuit of one-ports \(\mathcal{F}_1, \dotsc, \mathcal{F}_n\) is equivalent to a single one-port with I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\):

\[ \mathcal{F} = \{(V, I) \mid \exists I_1, \dotsc, I_n: (V, I_1) \in \mathcal{F}_1, \dotsc, (V, I_n) \in \mathcal{F}_n \text{ with } I = I_1 + \cdots + I_n\} \]

In other words, the voltage across the equivalent one-port is still \(V\), but the current \(I\) flowing through it is the sum of the currents flowing through \(\mathcal{F}_1, \dotsc, \mathcal{F}_n\):

\[ I = \sum_{k = 1}^n I_k \] Proof

TODO

Algorithm: Graphical Determining of the I-V Characteristic

We want to determine \(\mathcal{F}\) graphically:

  1. Draw \(\mathcal{F}_1, \dotsc, \mathcal{F}_n\) on the same I-V graph.
  2. Pick some voltage \(v\). Sum up the corresponding currents \(i_1, \dotsc, i_n\) of \(\mathcal{F}_1, \dotsc, \mathcal{F}_n\). The point \((v, i_1 + \cdots + i_n)\) is then part of \(\mathcal{F}\).
    • If any of \(\mathcal{F}_1, \dotsc, \mathcal{F}_n\) is not defined for \(v\), then \(\mathcal{F}\) is also not defined for \(v\)!
  3. Repeat step 2 a few times to get a few points of \(\mathcal{F}\). From these points you can roughly draw the graph of \(\mathcal{F}\).

docs.title: Linearization
docs.text:
Non-linear one-ports can have very complicated I-V characteristics, which often makes their analysis in the context of a particular circuit difficult. However, if we know that the one-port will only be operated within a small region around a specific point on its I-V characteristic, then it can be approximated very well as a linear one-port.

Definition: Linearization

Suppose we have a non-linear one-port with I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\) and a point \((v, i) \in \mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\).

Linearization is the process of finding a linear one-port whose I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{linear}}\) resembles \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\) as much as possible around the point \((v, i)\).

Theorem: Linearization via Implicit Representation

Suppose we have a non-linear one-port with I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\) and let \((v, i) \in \mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\).

If \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\) has an implicit representation \(f(V, I) = 0\), then the I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{linear}}\) of the linear one-port which best approximates \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\) around \((v, i)\) has an implicit representation which can be obtained using \(f\)'s partial derivatives:

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial V}(v, i) \cdot (V - v) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial I}(v, i) \cdot (I - i) = 0 \] Proof

TODO

Theorem: Linearization via Explicit Representation

Suppose we have a non-linear one-port with I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\) and let \((v, i) \in \mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\).

If \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\) has an explicit representation \(I = G(V)\), then the I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{linear}}\) of the linear one-port which best approximates \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\) around \((v, i)\) has an explicit representation which can be obtained using \(G\)'s derivative:

\[ I = G'(v) \cdot (V - v) + i \]

If \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\) has an explicit representation \(V = R(I)\), then the I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{linear}}\) of the linear one-port which best approximates \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{non-linear}}\) around \((v, i)\) has an explicit representation which can be obtained using \(R\)'s derivative:

\[ V = R'(i) \cdot (I - i) + v \] Proof

docs.title: One-Ports
docs.text:
Definition: One-Port

A one-port is a port with only two terminals.

By convention, we arbitrarily assign the names "positive" (+) and "negative" (-) to the terminals of each such one-port:

These names do not necessarily reflect which terminal is at a lower or higher electric potential, they are just labels. We could have just as easily called them "apple" and "banana". Once we have made this choice, we assign the reference direction of the voltage across each one-port to point from its positive terminal towards its negative terminal:

There are two possible conventions for the reference direction of the current flowing through each one-port: - In the passive sign convention (PSC), the reference arrow of the current is such that current flows into the positive terminal and out of the negative terminal. - In the active sign convention (ASC), the reference arrow of the current is such that current flows into the negative terminal and out of the positive terminal.

docs.title: Resistive Characteristic
docs.text:
Definition: Resistive Characteristic

The resistive characteristic of a one-port with general characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\) is the following set:

\[\mathcal{F}_R \overset{\text{def}}{=} \{(v, i) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid \exists q, \Phi \in \mathbb{R} \text{ such that } (v, i, q, \Phi) \in \mathcal{F}\}\]

docs.title: Resistance and Conductance
docs.text:
Definition: Static Resistance

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be the I-V characteristic of a one-port and let \((v, i) \in \mathcal{F}\).

The static resistance or chordal resistance of the one-port at \((v, i)\) is the ratio of the voltage \(v\) and the current \(i\):

\[ \frac{v}{i} \]

Notation

Static resistance is typically denoted by \(R\).

Unit: Ohm

Static resistance is measured in ohms with one ohm being equal to the ratio of one volt to one ampere:

\[ 1 \mathop{\Omega} = \frac{1 \mathop{\mathrm{V}}}{1 \mathop{\mathrm{A}}} \]

Definition: Static Conductance

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be the I-V characteristic of a one-port and let \((v, i) \in \mathcal{F}\).

The static conductance or chordal conductance of the one-port at \((v, v)\) is the ratio of the current \(i\) flowing and the voltage \(v\):

\[ \frac{i}{v} \]

Notation

Static conductance is typically denoted by \(G\).

Unit: Siemens

Static conductance is measured in siemens with one siemens being equal to the ratio of one ampere to one volt:

\[ 1 \mathop{\mathrm{S}} = \frac{1 \mathop{\mathrm{A}}}{1 \mathop{\mathrm{V}}} \]

Static resistance and static conductance are thus reciprocals:

\[ R = \frac{1}{G} \qquad G = \frac{1}{R} \]

Definition: Dynamic Resistance

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be the I-V characteristic of a one-port which has an implicit representation \(f(V, I) = 0\) and let \((v, i) \in \mathcal{F}\).

The dynamic resistance or differential resistance of the one-port at \((v, i)\) is the negative of the ration of \(f\)'s partial derivative with respect to \(I\) to \(f\)'s partial derivative with respect to \(V\):

\[ -\frac{\frac{\partial f}{\partial I} (v,i)}{\frac{\partial f}{\partial V} (v, i)} \]

Notation

Dynamic resistance is typically denoted in one of the following ways:

\[ r \qquad r_{\text{dyn}} \qquad r_{\text{diff}} \]

Unit: Ohm

Dynamic resistance is also measured in ohms, just like static resistance.

Definition: Dynamic Conductance

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be the I-V characteristic of a one-port which has an implicit representation \(f(V, I) = 0\) and let \((v, i) \in \mathcal{F}\).

The dynamic conductance or differential conductance of the one-port is the negative of the ration of \(f\)'s partial derivative with respect to \(V\) to \(f\)'s partial derivative with respect to \(I\):

\[ -\frac{\frac{\partial f}{\partial V} (v,i)}{\frac{\partial f}{\partial I} (v,i)} \]

Notation

Dynamic conductance is typically denoted in one of the following ways:

\[ g \qquad g_{\text{dyn}} \qquad g_{\text{diff}} \]

Unit: Ohm

Dynamic conductance is also measured in siemens, just like static conductance.

Dynamic resistance and dynamic conductance are thus reciprocals:

\[ r = \frac{1}{g} \qquad g = \frac{1}{r} \]

Theorem: Dynamic Resistance of Current-Driven One-Ports

The dynamic resistance of a current-driven one-port is \(V\)'s derivative with respect to \(I\):

\[ r = \frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}I} \] Proof

TODO

Theorem: Dynamic Conductance of Voltage-Driven One-Ports

The dynamic conductance of a voltage-driven one-port is \(I\)'s derivative with respect to \(V\):

\[ g = \frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}V} \] Proof

docs.title: Capacitive Characteristic
docs.text:
Definition: Capacitive Characteristic

The capacitive characteristic of a one-port with general characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\) is the following set:

\[\mathcal{F}_C \overset{\text{def}}{=} \{(v, q) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid \exists i, \Phi \in \mathbb{R} \text{ such that } (v, i, q, \Phi) \in \mathcal{F}\}\]

Definition: Voltage-Controlled Capacitive Characteristic

We say that \(\mathcal{F}\) is voltage-controlled if there exists some real function \(c\) such that

\[q = c(v) \qquad \forall(v, q) \in \mathcal{F}_C.\]

Definition: Charge-Controlled Capacitive Characteristic

We say that \(\mathcal{F}\) is charge-controlled if there exists some real function \(\chi\) such that

\[v = \chi(q) \qquad \forall (v, q) \in \mathcal{F}_C.\]

docs.title: Inductive Characteristic
docs.text:
Definition: Inductive Characteristic

The inductive characteristic of a one-port with general characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\) is the following set:

\[\mathcal{F}_L \overset{\text{def}}{=} \{(i, \Phi) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid \exists v, q \in \mathbb{R} \text{ such that } (v, i, q, \Phi) \in \mathcal{F}\}\]

Definition: Current-Controlled Inductive Characteristic

We say that \(\mathcal{F}_L\) is current-controlled if there exists some real function \(l\) such that

\[\Phi = l(i) \qquad \forall(i, \Phi) \in \mathcal{F}_L.\]

Definition: Flux-Controlled Inductive Characteristic

We say that \(\mathcal{F}_L\) is flux-controlled if there exists some real function \(\lambda\) such that

\[i = \lambda(\Phi) \qquad \forall (i, \Phi) \in \mathcal{F}_L.\]

docs.title: Memristive Characteristic
docs.text:
Definition: Memristive Characteristic

The memristive characteristic of a one-port with general characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\) is the following set:

\[\mathcal{F}_M \overset{\text{def}}{=} \{(\Phi, q) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid \exists v, i \in \mathbb{R} \text{ such that } (v, i, q, \Phi) \in \mathcal{F}\}\]

docs.title: Polarity
docs.text:
Some electronic components cannot operate when their terminals are not connected in a specific manner to the circuit. These are are known as polarized components

Definition: Unpolarized One-Port

A resistive one-port \(\mathcal{F}_R\) is unpolarized or bilateral if

\[(-v, -i) \in \mathcal{F}_R \qquad \forall (v, i) \in \mathcal{F}_R\]

Definition: Unpolarized One-Port

A resistive one-port \(\mathcal{F}_R\) is polarized or unilateral if it is not unpolarized:

\[\exists (v, i) \in \mathcal{F}_R \qquad \text{ such that } \qquad (-v, -i) \notin \mathcal{F}_R\]

When the terminals of a one-port are switched around, the mathematical descriptions of its voltage and current switch signs. If the one-port can operate at those new voltage and current, then it is unpolarized. If, however, there is a voltage and current such that the one-port cannot operate when their signs are switched, i.e. when the terminals of a one-port are switched around, then the one-port is polarized.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
When \(P(t) \gt 0\), then component is drawing energy. Conversely, when \(P(t) \lt 0\), the component is giving off energy. If \(P(t) = 0\), then the component is neither drawing nor giving off energy.

Theorem: Power of Resistive One-Ports

The power \(P(t)\) of resistive one-port at \(t\) is equal to the product of the current and voltage across it:

\[P(t) = v(t) \cdot i(t)\] Proof

TODO

Definition: Lossless Ports

A one-port with I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\) is lossless if it does not draw or give off energy at any current and voltage configuration:

\[VI = 0 \qquad \forall (V, I) \in \mathcal{F}\]

Tip

The I-V characteristic of a lossless port is restricted to one of the two axes because the current or the voltage must always be zero.

Definition: Lossy Ports

A one-port with I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\) is lossy if it there exists a current and voltage configuration at which it either draws or gives off energy:

\[ \exists (V, I) \qquad \text{such that} \qquad VI \ne 0 \]

Definition: Active Ports

A one-port with I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\) is active if it can be operated at a current and a voltage so as to give off energy:

\[ \exists (V, I) \in \mathcal{F} \qquad \text{such that} \qquad V I \lt 0 \]

Definition: Passive Ports

A one-port with I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\) is passive if it cannot be operated at a current and a voltage so as to give off energy:

\[ V I \ge 0 \qquad \forall (V, I) \in \mathcal{F} \]

Tip

The I-V characteristic of a passive port is restricted to the first and third quadrants because current and voltage must always have the same sign:

docs.title: Duality
docs.text:
Definition: Duality

We say that two one-ports with general characteristics \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{F}^d\) are dual if there exists some \(R_d \in \mathbb{R}\) such that

\[(q, \Phi, i, v) \in \mathcal{F} \iff (q^d, \Phi^d, i^d, v^d) \in \mathcal{F}^d,\]

where

\[q^d = \frac{1}{R_d}\Phi \qquad \Phi^d = R_d\cdot q \qquad i^d = \frac{1}{R_d}v \qquad v^d = R_d \cdot i.\]

Definition: Duality

We say that two resistive characteristics \(\mathcal{F}_R\) and \(\mathcal{F}_{R}^{d}\) are dual if there exists some \(k \in \mathbb{R}\) such that

\[(v, i) \in \mathcal{F}_R \iff (v^d, i^d) \in \mathcal{F}_{R}^{d},\]

where \(v^d = k\cdot I\) and \(i^d = \frac{1}{k}v\).

Definition: Duality

We say that a capacitive characteristic \(\mathcal{F}_C\) and \(\mathcal{F}_{R}^{d}\) are dual if there exists some \(k \in \mathbb{R}\) such that

\[(v, i) \in \mathcal{F}_R \iff (v^d, i^d) \in \mathcal{F}_{R}^{d},\]

where \(v^d = k\cdot I\) and \(i^d = \frac{1}{k}v\).

Theorem: Current-Driven and Voltage-Driven Dual Ports

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{F}_d\) be dual one-ports:

  • If \(\mathcal{F}\) is current-driven, then \(\mathcal{F}_d\) is voltage-driven with \(I_d = \frac{1}{D} f\left(\frac{1}{D}V_d\right)\).
  • If \(\mathcal{F}\) is voltage-driven, then \(\mathcal{F}_d\) is current-driven with \(V_d = D f(D I_d)\).
Proof

We need to prove two things:

  • (1) If \(\mathcal{F}\) is current-driven, then \(\mathcal{F}_d\) is voltage-driven.
  • (2) If \(\mathcal{F}\) is voltage-driven, then \(\mathcal{F}_d\) is current-driven.

Proof of (1):

Since \(\mathcal{F}\) is current-driven, we know that

\[ V = f(I). \]

Since \(V_d = D I\) and \(I_d = \frac{1}{D} V\), we know that \(V = D I_d\) and \(I = \frac{1}{D} V_d\). We thus get

\[ D I_d = f\left(\frac{1}{D}V_d\right) \] \[ I_d = \frac{1}{D} f\left(\frac{1}{D}V_d\right) \]

If we define \(g(V_d) = \frac{1}{D} f\left(\frac{1}{D}V_d\right)\), then

\[ I_d = g(V_d), \]

which makes \(\mathcal{F}_d\) voltage-driven.

Proof of (2):

Since \(\mathcal{F}\) is voltage-driven, we know that

\[ I = f(V). \]

Since \(V_d = D I\) and \(I_d = \frac{1}{D} V\), we know that \(V = D I_d\) and \(I = \frac{1}{D} V_d\). We thus get

\[ \frac{1}{D}V_d = f(D I_d) \] \[ V_d = D f(D I_d) \]

If we define \(g(I_d) = D f(D I_d)\), then

\[ I_d = g(V_d), \]

which makes \(\mathcal{F}_d\) current-driven.

Theorem: Polarity of Dual Ports

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{F}_d\) be dual one-ports:

  • If \(\mathcal{F}\) is polarized, then so is \(\mathcal{F}_d\).
  • If \(\mathcal{F}\) is unpolarized, then so is \(\mathcal{F}_d\).
Proof

Proof of (1):

TODO

Proof of (2):

Since \(\mathcal{F}\) is unpolarized, we know that \((-V, -I) \in \mathcal{F}\) for all \((V, I) \in \mathcal{F}\). Since \(V_d = DI\) and \(I_d = \frac{1}{D} V\), we know that \(-V_d = D(-I)\) and \(-I_d = \frac{1}{D}(-V)\). Therefore, \(-V_d\) is the dual of \(-I\) and \(-I_d\) is the dual of \(-V\), i.e. \((-V_d, -I_d) \in \mathcal{F}\).

Theorem: Power of Dual Ports

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{F}_d\) be dual one-ports:

  • If \(\mathcal{F}\) is lossless or lossy, then so is \(\mathcal{F}_d\).
  • If \(\mathcal{F}\) is passive or active, then so is \(\mathcal{F}_d\).
Proof

We need to prove four things:

  • If \(\mathcal{F}\) is lossless, then so is \(\mathcal{F}_d\).
  • If \(\mathcal{F}\) is lossy, then so is \(\mathcal{F}_d\).
  • If \(\mathcal{F}\) is passive, then so is \(\mathcal{F}_d\).
  • If \(\mathcal{F}\) is active, then so is \(\mathcal{F}_d\).

Proof of (1):

If \(\mathcal{F}\) is lossless, either \(V\) or \(I\) must always be zero. If \(V\) is always zero, then \(I_d\) will be always zero, since \(I_d = \frac{1}{D}V\). If \(I\) is always zero, then \(V_d\) will be always zero, since \(V_d = DI\). Therefore, \(I_d V_d\) will always be zero and so \(\mathcal{F}_d\) is also lossless.

Proof of (2):

If \(\mathcal{F}\) is lossy, there exist \((V, I) \in \mathcal{F}\) such that neither \(V\) nor \(I\) is zero. Since \(V_d = DI\) and \(I_d = \frac{1}{D}V\), we know that \(V_d\) and \(I_d\) would also be different from zero in this case and so \(V_d I_d \ne 0\), thus making \(\mathcal{F}_d\) also lossy.

Proof of (3):

If \(\mathcal{F}\) is passive, then \(V I \ge 0\). Since \(V_d = DI\) and \(I_d = \frac{1}{D}V\), we know that

\[ V_d I_d = DI \frac{1}{D}V = IU = UI \ge 0, \]

thus making \(\mathcal{F}_d\) also passive.

Proof of (4):

If \(\mathcal{F}\) is active, then there exist \((V, I) \in \mathcal{F}\) such that \(UI \lt 0\). Since \(V_d = DI\) and \(I_d = \frac{1}{D}V\), in this case we would have

\[ V_d I_d = DI \frac{1}{D}V = IU = UI \lt 0, \]

thus making \(\mathcal{F}_d\) also active.

docs.title: Time Invariance
docs.text:
Tip: Time Invariance

A time-invariant capacitive one-port is strictly linear if and only if its capacitive characteristic is a linear subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

Theorem: Work with Time-Invariant Strictly Linear Capacitive One-Ports

Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a time-invariant strictly linear capacitive one-port with capacitance \(C \ne 0\).

The work needed to change the charge of \(\mathcal{C}\) from \(Q_{\text{initial}}\) to \(Q_{\text{final}}\) is the following:

\[\frac{1}{2C}(Q_{\text{final}}^2 - Q_{\text{initial}}^2)\]

The work needed to change the voltage across \(\mathcal{C}\) from \(V_{\text{initial}}\) to \(V_{\text{final}}\) is the following:

\[\frac{1}{2}C(V_{\text{final}}^2 - V_{\text{initial}}^2)\] Proof

Theorem: Strictly Linear Capacitive One-Ports in Series

If \(n\) strictly linear capacitive one-ports with elastances \(S_1, \dotsc, S_n\) and capacitances \(C_1, \dotsc, C_n\), respectively, are connected in series, then they are equivalent to a single strictly linear capacitive one-port whose elastance \(S\) and capacitance \(C\) are given as follows:

\[S = \sum_{i=1}^n S_i = S_1 + S_2 + \cdots + S_n\] \[\frac{1}{C} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{C_i} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{C_n}\] Proof

Theorem: Strictly Linear Capacitive One-Ports in Parallel

If \(n\) strictly linear capacitive one-ports with capacitances \(C_1, \dotsc, C_n\) and elastances \(S_1, \dotsc, S_n\), respectively, are connected in parallel, then they are equivalent to a single strictly linear capacitive one-port whose capacitance \(C\) and elastance \(S\) are given as follows:

docs.title: Strictly Linear Inductive One-Ports
docs.text:
Theorem: Work with Time-Invariant Strictly Linear Inductive One-Ports

Let \(\mathcal{L}\) be a time-invariant strictly linear inductive one-port with inductance \(L \ne 0\).

The work needed to change the flux linkage of \(\mathcal{L}\) from \(\Phi_{\text{initial}}\) to \(\Phi_{\text{final}}\) is the following:

\[\frac{1}{2L}(\Phi_{\text{final}}^2 - \Phi_{\text{initial}}^2)\]

The work needed to change the current flowing through \(\mathcal{L}\) from \(I_{\text{initial}}\) to \(I_{\text{final}}\) is the following:

\[\frac{1}{2}L(I_{\text{final}}^2 - I_{\text{initial}}^2)\] Proof

\[L = \sum_{i=1}^n L_i = L_1 + L_2 + \cdots + L_n\] Proof

If \(n\) strictly linear resistive one-ports with resistances \(R_1, \dotsc, R_n\) and conductances \(G_1, \dotsc, G_n\), respectively, are connected in series, then they are equivalent to a single strictly linear resistive one-ports whose resistance \(R\) and conductance \(G\) are given as follows:

docs.title: Affine Two-Ports
docs.text:
Theorem: Strictly Linear Decomposition

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be an affine two-port.

If \(\mathcal{F}\) has an explicit representation

\[ \begin{bmatrix}p_1 \\ p_2\end{bmatrix} = \boldsymbol{M}\begin{bmatrix}q_1 \\ q_2\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}P_1 \\ P_2\end{bmatrix}, \]

then it is equivalent to a strictly linear two-port \(\mathcal{F}'\) whose corresponding representation matrix is \(\boldsymbol{M}\) and which has independent time-invariant ideal sources attached to it in the following configuration:

  • If \(p_k\) is the current flowing into the \(j\)-th port of \(\mathcal{F}\), then a DC source is attached at the \(j\)-th port so that the current flowing into the \(j\)-th port of \(\mathcal{F}'\) is \(i_j - P_k\).
  • If \(p_k\) is the voltage across the \(j\)-th port of \(\mathcal{F}\), then a voltage source is attached at the \(j\)-th port so that the voltage across the \(j\)-th port of \(\mathcal{F}'\) is \(v_j - P_k\).

Proof

docs.title: Linear Two-Ports
docs.text: A two-port is strictly linear if its I-V characteristic is a two-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^4\).

docs.title: Representations
docs.text:
Info: Implicit Representation

A strictly linear two-port has an implicit representation

\[ \boldsymbol{M} \boldsymbol{v} + \boldsymbol{N} \boldsymbol{i} = \boldsymbol{0}, \]

where \(\boldsymbol{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}\) and \(\boldsymbol{N} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}\).

Info: Parametric Representation

A strictly linear two-port has a parametric representation

\[ \begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{v} \\ \boldsymbol{i}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{V} \\ \boldsymbol{I}\end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\lambda} \]

where \(\boldsymbol{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}\) and \(\boldsymbol{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}\).

docs.title: Reciprocity
docs.text:
Theorem: Reciprocity Based on Elements

If a two-port does not contain any elements other than linear resistors, transformers, capacitors and inductors, then it is reciprocal.

Proof

TODO

Theorem: Ratios of Reciprocal Two-Ports

Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a strictly linear two-port.

If \(\mathcal{F}\) is reciprocal, then we have the following properties:

  • The ratio of \(v_1\) to \(v_2\) whenever \(i_1 = 0\) is the same as the negative of the ratio of \(i_2\) to \(i_1\) whenever \(v_2 = 0\).
\[ \left.\frac{v_1}{v_2}\right\vert_{i_1 = 0} = \left.-\frac{i_2}{i_1}\right\vert_{v_2 = 0} \]
  • The ratio of \(v_2\) to \(v_1\) whenever \(i_2 = 0\) is the same as the negative of the ratio of \(i_1\) to \(i_2\) whenever \(v_1 = 0\).
\[ \left.\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right\vert_{i_2 = 0} = \left. -\frac{i_1}{i_2}\right\vert_{v_1 = 0} \] Proof

Theorem: Reciprocity via Transmission Representation

If \(\mathcal{F}\) has a forwards transmission matrix \(\boldsymbol{T}\), then it is reciprocal if and only if the determinant of \(\boldsymbol{T}\) is \(1\):

\[ \det \boldsymbol{T} = 1 \] Proof

docs.title: Symmetry
docs.text:
Theorem: Symmetry via Admittance Representation

A strictly linear two-port with admittance representation

\[ \boldsymbol{i} = \boldsymbol{G} \boldsymbol{v} \]

is symmetrical if and only if

\[ \boldsymbol{G} = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{G}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}, \]

i.e. \(\boldsymbol{G}\) remains the same if you swap the elements on its diagonals.

Proof

Theorem: Symmetry via Impedance Representation

A strictly linear two-port with impedance representation

\[ \boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{R} \boldsymbol{i} \]

is symmetrical if and only if

\[ \boldsymbol{R} = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{R}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}, \]

i.e. \(\boldsymbol{R}\) remains the same if you swap the elements on its diagonals.

Proof

Theorem: Symmetry via Transmission Representations

A strictly linear two-port with existing forwards transmission representation

\[ \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ i_1 \end{bmatrix} = \boldsymbol{T} \begin{bmatrix}v_2 \\ -i_2\end{bmatrix} \]

and backwards transmission representation

\[ \begin{bmatrix} v_2 \\ i_2 \end{bmatrix} = \boldsymbol{T}' \begin{bmatrix}v_1 \\ -i_1\end{bmatrix} \]

is symmetrical if and only if

\[ \boldsymbol{T} = \boldsymbol{T}'. \] Proof

docs.title: Nullors
docs.text:
Definition: Nullor

A nullor is a strictly linear two-port which has the following implicit representation:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{v} + \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{i} = \boldsymbol{0} \]

Notation

The symbol for the nullor is the following:

It looks like this because a nullor is equivalent to a nullator and a norator, since \(v_1 = 0\) and \(i_1 = 0\), but we don't know anything about \(v_2\) and \(i_2\).

Info: Transmission Representation

The transmission representation of the nullor is the following:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}v_1 \\ i_1\end{bmatrix} = \boldsymbol{T} \begin{bmatrix}v_2 \\ -i_2\end{bmatrix} \qquad \boldsymbol{T} = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \]

It is the only explicit representation which exists for the nullor.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: We can connect two-ports in ways similar to one-ports.

docs.title: Series-Series Connection
docs.text:
Definition: Series-Series Connection

Two two-ports are series-series connected when their input ports are connected in series with one another and their output ports are also connected in series with one another:

In a series-series connection, we have the following:

\[ \boldsymbol{i}_{\mathcal{F}_1} = \boldsymbol{i}_{\mathcal{F}_2} \]

Theorem: Series-Series Equivalent

Two two-ports \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) in a series-series connection are equivalent to a single two-port \(\mathcal{F}\):

We have the following:

\[ \boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}} = \boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}_1} = \boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}_2} \qquad \boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}} = \boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}_1} + \boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}_2} \]

If \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) have impedance representations \(\boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}_1} = R_1 (\boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}_1})\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}_2} = R_2 (\boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}_2})\), then \(\mathcal{F}\) also has an impedance representation

\[ \boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}} = R(\boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}}), \]

where \(R\) is the sum of the functions \(R_1\) and \(R_2\):

\[ R = R_1 + R_2 \] Proof

TODO

docs.title: Series-Parallel Connection
docs.text:
Definition: Series-Parallel Connection

Two two-ports are series-parallel connected when their input ports are connected in series with one another and their output ports are connected in parallel with one another:

In a series-parallel connection, we have the following:

\[ i_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} = i_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \qquad v_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} = v_2^{\mathcal{F}_2} \]

Theorem: Series-Parallel Equivalent

Two two-ports \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) in a series-parallel connection are equivalent to a single two-port \(\mathcal{F}\):

We have the following:

\[ \begin{aligned}i_1^{\mathcal{F}} &= i_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} = i_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ \\ v_1^{\mathcal{F}} &= v_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} + v_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \end{aligned} \qquad \qquad \begin{aligned} i_2^{\mathcal{F}} &= i_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} + i_2^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ \\ v_2^{\mathcal{F}} &= v_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} = v_2^{\mathcal{F}_2}\end{aligned} \]

If \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) have hybrid representations \(\begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} \\ i_2^{\mathcal{F}_1}\end{bmatrix} = H_1 \left(\begin{bmatrix}i_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} \\ v_2^{\mathcal{F}_1}\end{bmatrix}\right)\) and \(\begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ i_2^{\mathcal{F}_2}\end{bmatrix} = H_2 \left(\begin{bmatrix}i_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ v_2^{\mathcal{F}_2}\end{bmatrix}\right)\), then \(\mathcal{F}\) also has a hybrid representation

\[ \begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}} \\ i_2^{\mathcal{F}}\end{bmatrix} = H \left(\begin{bmatrix}i_1^{\mathcal{F}} \\ v_2^{\mathcal{F}}\end{bmatrix}\right), \]

where \(H\) is the sum of the functions \(H_1\) and \(H_2\):

\[ H = H_1 + H_2 \] Proof

TODO

docs.title: Parallel-Series Connection
docs.text:
Definition: Parallel-Series Connection

Two two-ports are parallel-series connected when their input ports are connected in parallel with one another and their output ports are connected in series with one another:

In a parallel-series connection, we have the following:

\[ v_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} = v_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \qquad i_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} = i_2^{\mathcal{F}_2} \]

Theorem: Parallel-Series Equivalent

Two two-ports \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) in a parallel-series connection are equivalent to a single two-port \(\mathcal{F}\):

We have the following:

\[ \begin{aligned}i_1^{\mathcal{F}} &= i_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} + i_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ \\ v_1^{\mathcal{F}} &= v_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} = v_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \end{aligned}\qquad \qquad\begin{aligned}i_2^{\mathcal{F}} &= i_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} = i_2^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ \\ v_2^{\mathcal{F}} &= v_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} + v_2^{\mathcal{F}_2}\end{aligned} \]

If \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) have inverse hybrid representations \(\begin{bmatrix}i_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} \\ v_2^{\mathcal{F}_1}\end{bmatrix} = H_1' \left(\begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} \\ i_2^{\mathcal{F}_1}\end{bmatrix}\right)\) and \(\begin{bmatrix}i_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ v_2^{\mathcal{F}_2}\end{bmatrix} = H_2' \left(\begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ i_2^{\mathcal{F}_2}\end{bmatrix}\right)\), then \(\mathcal{F}\) also has an inverse hybrid representation

\[ \begin{bmatrix}i_1^{\mathcal{F}} \\ v_2^{\mathcal{F}}\end{bmatrix} = H' \left(\begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}} \\ i_2^{\mathcal{F}}\end{bmatrix}\right), \]

where \(H'\) is the sum of the functions \(H_1'\) and \(H_2'\):

\[ H' = H_1' + H_2' \] Proof

TODO

docs.title: Parallel-Parallel Connection
docs.text:
Definition: Parallel-Parallel Connection

Two two-ports are parallel-parallel connected when their input ports are connected in parallel with one another and their output ports are also connected in parallel with one another:

In a parallel-parallel connection, we have the following:

\[ \boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}_1} = \boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}_2} \]

Theorem: Parallel-Parallel Equivalent

Two two-ports \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) in a parallel-parallel connection are equivalent to a single two-port \(\mathcal{F}\):

We always have:

\[ \boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}} = \boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}_1} = \boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}_2} \qquad \boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}} = \boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}_1} + \boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}_2} \]

If \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) have admittance representations \(\boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}_1} = G_1(\boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}_1})\) and \(\boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}_2} = G_2(\boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}_2})\), then \(\mathcal{F}\) also has an admittance representation:

\[ \boldsymbol{i}^{\mathcal{F}} = G(\boldsymbol{v}^{\mathcal{F}}), \]

where \(G\) is the sum of the functions \(G_1\) and \(G_2\):

\[ G = G_1 + G_2 \] Proof

TODO

docs.title: Cascade Connection
docs.text:
Definition: Cascade Connection

Two two-ports are cascade connected when the output port of the first is connected to the input port of the second:

We have the following:

\[ v_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} = v_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \qquad i_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} = - i_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \]

Theorem: Cascade Equivalent

Two two-ports \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) in a cascade connection are equivalent to a single two-port \(\mathcal{F}\):

We have the following:

\[ \begin{aligned} v_1^{\mathcal{F}} &= v_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} \\ \\ i_1^{\mathcal{F}} &= i_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} \end{aligned} \qquad \qquad \begin{aligned} v_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} &= v_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ \\ i_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} &= -i_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \end{aligned} \qquad \qquad \begin{aligned} v_2^{\mathcal{F}} &= v_2^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ \\ i_2^{\mathcal{F}} &= i_2^{\mathcal{F}_2} \end{aligned} \]

If \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) have forwards transmission representations \(\begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} \\ i_1^{\mathcal{F}_1}\end{bmatrix} = T_1 \left(\begin{bmatrix}v_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} \\ -i_2^{\mathcal{F}_1}\end{bmatrix}\right)\) and \(\begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ i_1^{\mathcal{F}_2}\end{bmatrix} = T_2 \left(\begin{bmatrix}v_2^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ -i_2^{\mathcal{F}_2}\end{bmatrix}\right)\), then \(\mathcal{F}\) also has a forwards transmission representation

\[ \begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}} \\ i_1^{\mathcal{F}}\end{bmatrix} = T \left(\begin{bmatrix}v_2^{\mathcal{F}} \\ -i_2^{\mathcal{F}}\end{bmatrix}\right), \]

where \(T\) is the composition of the functions \(T_1\) and \(T_2\):

\[ T = T_1 \circ T_2 \]

If \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) have backwards transmission representations \(\begin{bmatrix}v_2^{\mathcal{F}_1} \\ i_2^{\mathcal{F}_1}\end{bmatrix} = T_1' \left(\begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}_1} \\ -i_1^{\mathcal{F}_1}\end{bmatrix}\right)\) and \(\begin{bmatrix}v_2^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ i_2^{\mathcal{F}_2}\end{bmatrix} = T_2' \left(\begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}_2} \\ -i_1^{\mathcal{F}_2}\end{bmatrix}\right)\), then \(\mathcal{F}\) also has a backwards transmission representation

\[ \begin{bmatrix}v_2^{\mathcal{F}} \\ i_2^{\mathcal{F}}\end{bmatrix} = T' \left(\begin{bmatrix}v_1^{\mathcal{F}} \\ -i_1^{\mathcal{F}}\end{bmatrix}\right), \]

where \(T\) is the composition of the functions \(T_2\) and \(T_1\):

\[ T' = T_2' \circ T_1' \] Proof

docs.title: Two-Ports
docs.text:
Definition: Two-Port

A two-port is a port with four terminals.

Definition: Input Port

The port with \(i_1\) is known as the input port.

Definition: Output Port

The port with \(i_2\) is known as the output port.

docs.title: I-V Characteristic
docs.text:
The I-V characteristic of a two-port reduces to the following set, where \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) are the I-V characteristics of the constituent one-ports:

\[ \mathcal{F} \overset{\text{def}} = \left\{ \left( \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}i_1 \\ i_2\end{bmatrix}\right) : (v_1, i_1) \in \mathcal{F}_1 \text{ and } (v_2, i_2) \in \mathcal{F}_2 \right\} \]

docs.title: Representations
docs.text:
We define four additional explicit representations of the I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\) of a two-port:

Definition: Hybrid Representation

A hybrid representation is any function \(h\) with the following property:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}v_1 \\ i_2\end{bmatrix} = H\left(\begin{bmatrix} i_1 \\ v_2 \end{bmatrix}\right) \]

Definition: Hybrid Matrix

If \(H\) is a linear transformation, then its standard matrix representation is known as a hybrid matrix and its components as hybrid parameters.

Definition: Inverse Hybrid Representation

An inverse hybrid representation is any function \(H^{-1}\) with the following property:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}i_1 \\ v_2\end{bmatrix} = H'\left(\begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\\ i_2 \end{bmatrix}\right) \]

Notation

Sometimes, we also denote \(H'\) by \(H^{-1}\).

Definition: Inverse Hybrid Matrix

If \(H^{-1}\) is a linear transformation, then its standard matrix representation is known as an inverse hybrid matrix and its components as inverse hybrid parameters.

Definition: Forwards Transmission Representation

A forwards transmission representation is any function \(T\) with the following property:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ i_1 \end{bmatrix} = T\left(\begin{bmatrix}v_2 \\ -i_2\end{bmatrix}\right) \]

Definition: Forwards Transmission Matrix

If \(T\) is a linear transformation, then its standard matrix representation is known as a forwards transmission matrix and its components as forwards transmission parameters.

Definition: Backwards Transmission Representation

An backwards transmission representation is any function \(T^{-1}\) with the following property:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} v_2 \\ -i_2 \end{bmatrix} = T'\left(\begin{bmatrix}v_1 \\ i_1\end{bmatrix}\right) \]

Notation

Sometimes, we also denote \(T'\) by \(T^{-1}\).

Definition: Backwards Transmission Matrix

If \(T\) is a linear transformation, then its standard matrix representation is known as a backwards transmission matrix and its components as backwards transmission parameters.

Warning:

Some questionable people define the backwards transmission representation in the following non-equivalent way:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} v_2 \\ i_2 \end{bmatrix} = T'\left(\begin{bmatrix}v_1 \\ -i_1\end{bmatrix}\right) \]

docs.title: Symmetry
docs.text:
Definition: Symmetry

A two-port with I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\) is symmetrical or reversible if is has the following property:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}v_1 \\ v_2 \\ i_1 \\ i_2\end{bmatrix} \in \mathcal{F} \implies \begin{bmatrix}v_2 \\ v_1 \\ i_2 \\ i_1\end{bmatrix} \in \mathcal{F} \]

Intuitively, a symmetrical two-port is one for which the input and output are indistinguishable. It behaves the same way if you "turn it around".

Definition: Antisymmetry

A two-port with I-V characteristic \(\mathcal{F}\) is antisymmetrical if it is dual to some two-port \(\mathcal{F}^d\) with the following property:

\[ \begin{bmatrix}v_1 \\ v_2 \\ i_1 \\ i_2\end{bmatrix} \in \mathcal{F} \implies \begin{bmatrix}v_2 \\ v_1 \\ i_2 \\ i_1\end{bmatrix} \in \mathcal{F}_d \]

Intuitively, an antisymmetrical two-port is one for which the reversing the input and output results in one of its dual two-ports, i.e. it behaves as one of its duals when you "turn it around".

docs.title: PCB Design Rules
docs.text:
PCB design rules are the set of constraints one must adhere to when designing and laying out a PCB. Setting up PCB design rules should be the first step in the design process after specifying the stack-up. The vast majority of these rules will be based on the manufacturer's capabilities, since they pertain to physical constraints, while the rest of the rules are a consequence of the desired functionality.

Tip: Avoid Absolute Limits

Manufacturers always specify the absolute limits which they are capable of. However, one should avoid these as much as possible because they come with lower yields and increased costs.

docs.title: Clearance Constraints
docs.text:
Clearance constraints are the minimum allowable distances between various things on a PCB. These are based on the manufacturer's capabilities. Unless strictly required by the design, one should always add a safety margin on top of the limits listed by the manufacturer.

Tip: Safety Margin Rule of Thumb

  • Trace / pad / polygon pour to trace / pad / polygon pour: +0.025 to +0.05 mm (+1 to +2 mils).
  • Trace / pad / polygon pour to via / hole: +0.075 to +0.125mm (+3 to +5 mils).
  • Exposed copper to silkscreen: +0.05 to +0.075 mm (+2 to +3 mils).
  • Copper to board edge: +0.25 to +0.50 mm.

One common way to specify clearance constraints in CAD software is using a table known as a clearance matrix. Each type of object which the constraint can apply to is assigned both a row and a column. The value inside a cell is what specifies the constraint for the minimum allowed distance between the types of objects corresponding to the cell's row and column.

Example: Altium Clearance Matrix

Following is a clearance matrix inside Altium Designer (values should not be taken seriously).

docs.title: Size Constraints
docs.text:
Size constraints are the allowable sizes for the various things on a PCB. These are based on the manufacturer's capabilities and are typically specified as a minimum and often also a maximum value. Most CAD software also have offer the option to specify a "preferred" value in the range between the minimum and maximum. This is then used simply as the default for various operations like placing new traces or vias. A safety margin should be added to the manufacturer's minimum or subtracted from the maximum, respectively.

Tip: Safety Margin Rule of Thumb

  • Minimum trace width: +0.025 to +0.05 mm (+1 to +2 mils).
  • Minimum diameter of mechanically drilled hole: +0.10 mm (+4 mils).
  • Minimum annular ring size: +0.05 mm (+2 mils).
  • Minimum SMD pad size: +0.05 mm per edge (+2 mils per edge).

docs.title: Printed Circuit Board
docs.text:
A printed circuit board (PCB) is a sandwich-like structure used for connecting electronic components in a unified circuit. Each PCB comprises a stack of insulating and conductive layers in an alternating pattern:

A single PCB can feature anywhere between 1 layer and a few dozen layers. The primary characteristics of each layer are its type (insulating or conductive), its thickness and the dielectric constant of its dielectric material.

Each insulating layer is essentially a rectangular block made of dielectric material. These layers provide the structural backbone of the PCB and are what holds it together. With the exception of vias passing through them, they are not allowed to contain any electrical connections.

A conductive layer represents space which can be occupied by electrical connections. These connections are exclusively made of copper with purity ≥99.8 %. Conductive layers are what enable electronic components to communicate with each other. The space within conductive layers which is not occupied by copper is occupied by a dielectric, just like insulating layers.

For insulating layers, the thickness is given in mils or millimeters. However, in the context of conductive layers, thickness is called copper weight and is specified in ounces per square foot (oz/ft²), although this is ubiquitously written as just oz. Specifically, a copper weight of "\(x\) oz" corresponds to the thickness of a copper sheet which you would get if you took exactly \(x\) ounces of raw copper and rolled them out perfectly flat to cover an area of exactly 1 square foot.

Example: Commonly Used Copper Weights

Below is a table of some commonly used copper weights with the physical thicknesses they correspond to in both mils (thousandths of an inch) and millimeters:

Copper Weight Thickness (mils) Thickness (mm) 0.5 oz 0.69 mils ≈0.0175 mm 1.0 oz 1.37 mils ≈0.035 mm 2.0 oz 2.74 mils ≈0.070 mm

A very common standard is 1 oz for the two outer conductive layers and 0.5 oz for inner conductive layers.

The other important characteristic to consider, especially for insulating layers, is the dielectric constant. Different insulating layers may be made of slightly different materials which have different dielectric constants. For conductive layers, the space which is not occupied with copper is filled with the same material as the surrounding insulating layers.

docs.title: Build-Up
docs.text:
The build-up of a PCB refers to the physical organization of its layers, specifically:

  • the total number of layers;
  • the total thickness of the PCB;
  • the characteristics of each layer.

Choosing a build-up is the first step in the PCB layout process and should be done with careful consideration of the physical and functional constraints of the target product. Each manufacturer has their own set of "standard" build-ups which they support. Choosing a non-standard build-up necessitates consultation with the manufacturer to check if it is manufacturable in the first place and usually comes with additional manufacturing costs.

Some typical total thicknesses are 1.6 mm and 1.2 mm, although it is possible to also manufacture PCB's as thin as 0.8 mm and as thick as several millimeters.

docs.title: Stack-Up
docs.text:
Stack-up refers to the assignment of roles to the conductive layers in a given PCB:

  • Signal layers are used for electrical connections which are relevant to the functions of components.
  • Ground layers are used as the common reference point for voltages in the PCB. Usually, they are completely filled with copper in order to provide low resistance and direct access to ground through vias. Apart from only the simplest designs, every PCB has at least one such layer.
  • Power layers are used for providing direct access to power through vias.
  • Mixed layers are used for any of the above. It is common to compartmentalize them in a way where each physical region of the layer serves a specific purpose.

Since both ground layers and power layers are typically filled with copper as much as possible, they also serve as protection from electromagnetic interference.

Note

Many people also use the term "stack-up" for both the build-up and the stack-up.

docs.title: Solder Mask
docs.text: The two outer-most layers of a PCB are the so-called solder mask or solder resist. They serve as a means to protect

docs.title: Traces
docs.text:
A trace in a PCB is a thin segment of conductive material in a conductive layer (typically copper) which connects electronic components.

The three most important physical characteristics of a trace are its length, width and thickness and they play a great role in determining the electrical properties of the trace.

Tip: Trapezoidal Cross-Section

The manufacturing process actually makes traces with a trapezoidal cross-section but we can treat it as rectangular to a great approximation.

The thickness of a trace is the copper weight of the conductive layer in which it resides. The only way to change it is to use a different build-up, but this is rarely a good strategy. Instead, one should rely on varying the width and the length to achieve the desired goals.

A typical width can range anywhere from 0.1 mm to 1.0 mm. Each manufacturer has their own minimum width which they support, but this limit should be avoided because it comes with increased costs and lower yields. The width for a given trace should be chosen according to its purpose. Common widths are in the range of 0.2 mm - 0.3 mm (~10 mils) for signal traces and 0.5 mm - 1.0 mm (~20 mils) for power traces (including ground), but these are only rough guidelines. In fact, certain applications like controlled impedance require the strict calculation of a specific width.

The length of a trace also has a great effect on its electrical properties. In the vast majority of cases, traces should be kept as short as possible because additional length increases the emission of and susceptibility to interference. However, artificially increasing the length of a trace is commonly done when specific signal timing requirements need to be met.

docs.title: Current Handling
docs.text:
Traces heat up as current passes through them and it is often necessary to keep their temperature within a given range. This is done by calculating an appropriate trace width based on the maximum continuous current the trace needs to sustain and the maximum permissible temperature rise. There are many online calculators which can do this.

Furthermore, each trace itself has an absolute maximum continuous current which it can sustain, mainly based on its physical dimensions. Exceeding this limit can cause such a high temperature that the trace itself can start melting or burn up.

docs.title: Theoretical Modelling
docs.text:
Despite the physical simplicity of traces, modelling their electrical properties is actually fairly complicated. In the simplest of designs, a trace can be modelled as a short circuit, but this model reaches its limit really quickly.

A more accurate model treats the trace as an RL series circuit between the two connected components:

TODO: Diagram

The resistance \(R\) is given by the resistivity \(\rho\) of copper, the cross-sectional area \(A\) of the trace as well as its length \(l\). By treating the cross-section as a rectangle, its area \(A\) can be approximated using the trace's width \(w\) and thickness \(h\):

\[R = \frac{\rho \cdot l}{A} = \frac{\rho \cdot l}{w \cdot h}\]

Calculating the inductance \(L\) is more involved but for frequencies of up to a few MHz, \(L\) can be approximated using the Rosa-Grover formula:

\[L = 0.2\cdot l \left( 0.5 + \frac{0.2235 \cdot (w + h)}{l} + \ln \frac{2l}{w + h} \right)\]

Here, \(L\) is nH, while the width \(w\), length \(l\) and thickness \(h\) are in mm. We see that \(L\) is dominated by \(h\): a longer trace as more inductance.

docs.title: Via
docs.text:
A vertical interconnect access (via) is a tunnel inside the structure of a PCB which connects two or more conductive layers.

The outline of the tunnel is called the barrel and is made of copper. Connections to conductive layers happen via rings of copper around the barrel known as an annular rings.

The most main mechanical characteristics of a via are the following:

  • via diameter / drill diameter- the diameter of the opening inside the tunnel;
  • annular ring width (often just called annular ring) - the distance between the inner and the outer edge of an annular ring;
  • pad diameter - the distance from the center of the opening to the outer edge of an annular ring.

docs.title: Tenting
docs.text:
Tenting is the process of covering an exposed via opening and its annular ring with solder mask.

The main advantage of tenting is that it isolates the via from the external environment, thus preventing solder bridges and short circuits. It is very common in production boards. However, tenting is usually avoided during prototyping to allow vias to serve as testing pads.

On its own, tenting does not involve additional costs and is generally reliable for vias with a drill diameter of up to \(0.38\,\mathrm{mm}\) (\(15 \,\mathrm{mil}\)). Some manufacturers may be able to tent larger vias, but the process becomes increasingly error prone because solder mask can drip into the barrel instead of covering the opening. This can cause various defects during assembly and even after that by gradually corroding the via from the inside. Such vias should be plugged instead of tented.

docs.title: Sinusoidal Signals
docs.text:
Definition: Sinusoidal Signal

A sinusoidal signal is a real function \(x: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) which can be expressed as

\[x(t) = X_{\text{max}} \cos(\omega t + \phi)\]

for some \(X_\)

docs.title: Phasors
docs.text:
Definition: Phasors

The phasor of a sinusoidal signal

\[x(t) = X_{\text{m}}\cos(\omega t + \phi)\]

is the complex number given by the multiplication of the amplitude \(X_{\text{m}}\) with the complex exponential \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{j}\phi}\):

\[X \overset{\text{def}}{=} X_m \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{j}\phi}\]

Theorem: Signal from Phasor

A sinusoidal signal

\[x(t) = X_{\text{m}}\cos(\omega t + \phi)\]

is equal to the real part of the multiplication of its phasor \(X\) by \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{j}\omega t}\):

\[x(t) = \operatorname{Re} (X \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{j} \omega t})\] Proof

TODO

Theorem: Signal Equality \(\iff\) Phasor Equality

Two sinusoidal signals are identical if and only if their phasors are the same.

Proof

TODO

Theorem: Linearity of the Phasor Transform

If a sinusoidal signal \(x(t)\) can be expressed as a linear combination

\[x(t) = \sum_{k=1}^n \lambda_k x_k(t)\]

of sinusoidal signals \(x_1(t), \dotsc, x_n(t)\) with the same frequency, then its phasor can be expressed as a linear combination of their phasors \(X_1, \dotsc, X_n\) with the same coefficients:

\[X = \sum_{k=1}^n \lambda_k X_k\] Proof

TODO

Theorem: Differentiation and Phasors

If a sinusoidal signal

\[x(t) = X_{\text{m}} \cos(\omega t + \phi)\]

has the phasor \(X\), then its derivative has the following phasor:

\[\mathrm{j}\omega X\] Proof

TODO

Theorem: Antidifferentiation and Phasors

If a sinusoidal signal

\[x(t) = X_{\text{m}} \cos(\omega t + \phi)\]

has the phasor \(X\), then its antiderivative has the following phasor:

\[\frac{1}{\mathrm{j}\omega} X\] Proof

docs.title: Cyrillic Script
docs.text: The Cyrillic script is a writing system which was developed during the late 9th century in the Preslav Literary School of the First Bulgarian Empire by the disciples of Cyril and Methodius - creators of the [[TODO|Glagolitic script]]. It was historically used for writing Old Church Slavonic and still remains in use for writing Church Slavonic. Additionally, variations of the Cyrillic script are currently used by around 250 million people in Eurasia as the official scripts for their national languages.

docs.title: Orthography (Arabic)
docs.text:
The writing system used by the Arabic language is an abjad consisting of 28 letters. It is a cursive script written from right to left and top to bottom. All letters have between two and four forms depending on their position in a word so as to be able to connect with the letters surrounding them: - The initial form is used at the start of a word and connects with the letter after it. - The medial form is used in the middle of a word and connects with the letters before and after it. - The final form is used at the end of a word and connects with the letter preceding it.

The letters ʾalif (ا), dāl (د), dhāl (ذ), rāʾ (ر), zayn (ز), and wāw (و) are known as non-connecting letters. They only have two forms and do not connect to a subsequent letter in the word. Any letter that follows them must begin a new connection, taking its initial form (or isolated form if it is the last letter of the word).

All letters except for ʾalif (ا), wāw (و) and yāʾ (ي) denote a single consonant sound. The letters wāw (و) and yāʾ (ي) can denote either the consonants /w/ and /j/ or the long vowels /uː/ and /iː/, respectively. The letter ʾalif (ا) does not have its own pronunciation. Instead, it can represent a few different sounds depending on how its used.

Note: Spelling Variants of ʾalif (ا)

The letter ʾalif (ا) has two additional spelling variants:

  • Dagger ʾAlif (الألف الخنجرية, al-ʾAlif al-Khanjariyyah) is a short diacritic (ـٰ) used to indicate that the consonant on which it is placed is followed by the long vowel /aː/. This is used only in a few words such as الله (Allāh) in the Quran. Outside of the Quran, it is rarely used.
  • ʾAlif Maqṣūrah (الأَلِف المَقْصُورَة) only occurs at a word-final position and looks like a dotless yāʾ (ى). It is pronounced as long vowel /aː/ and is used only in specific situations.
Note: تَاء مَرْبُوطَة (tā' marbūṭa)

There is a special variant of the letter tā' known as تَاء مَرْبُوطَة (tā' marbūṭa). It can only occur at the end of words. It is written as ﺔ when linked to the previous letter and as ة when unlinked. The pronunciation of tā' marbūṭa varies:

  • In full form, it is pronounced as /t/ (e.g. سَيَّارَةٌ, sayyāratun).
  • In pause form, it is pronounced as /h/ (e.g. سَيَّارَةْ sayyārah). However, if the word is the first word of an [[TODO|إضافة]], then it is again pronounced as /t/.

Short vowels are almost never written in practice. Speakers have to rely on contextual cues to determine which vowels to pronounce. However, there is a system of diacritics, known as vocalization, which is used to indicate short vowels in specific contexts.

docs.title: Vocalization
docs.text:
A system of diacritics known as vocalization is used to show the pronunciation of short vowels:

Diacritic IPA Name ـَ /a/ فَتْحَة fatḥah ـِ /i/ كَسْرَة kasrah ـُ /u/ ضَمَّة ḍammah ــْـ /ø/ سُكُون sukūn

When such a diacritic is placed on any letter except ʾalif (ا), wāw (و) and yāʾ (ي), it indicates that the consonant should be pronounced followed by the respective short vowel. When placed on wāw (و) or yāʾ (ي), the diacritic indicates /w/ or /j/ + the short vowel, respectively.

In vocalized texts, long vowels are indicated by the following combinations of ʾalif (ا), wāw (و) or yāʾ (ي) (without diacritics) and the respective diacritic placed on the letter preceding ʾalif (ا), wāw (و) or yāʾ (ي): - The long vowel /a:/ is indicated by ا and a fat·ḥah on the letter before ا; - The long vowel /u:/ is indicated by و and a ḍammah on the consonant before و. - The long vowel /i:/ is indicated by ي and a kasrah on the consonant before ي;

The sukūn is a special diacritic which indicates that there is no vowel after the letter.

Note: Use of Vocalization

Vocalization is almost never used in practice. It is only used in the Quran and when teaching the language. Rarely, it might also be used to resolve ambiguity.

docs.title: Tanwīn
docs.text:
Three additional diacritics known as تَنوِين (tanwīn) may occur on word-final letters. They indicate that the letter should be pronounced followed by a particular short vowel + /n/. The use of tanwīn is governed by the grammatical rules of [[TODO|nunation]].

Diacritic IPA Name ـً /an/ فَتْحَتَيْنِ fatḥahtayn ـٍ /in/ كَسْرَتَيْنِ kasratayn ـٌ /un/ ضَمَّتَيْنِ ḍammatayn

docs.title: Hamza
docs.text:
The symbol ء is known as هَمْزة (hamza) and is used to indicate a [[TODO|glottal stop]] /ʔ/. It can appear either on its own like a separate letter or as a diacritic on a "seat": one of ʾalif (ا), wāw (و) and yāʾ (ي). When used as seats for hamza, the letters ʾalif (ا), wāw (و) and yāʾ (ي) themselves do not denote any sound. Furthermore, yāʾ (ي) loses its two dots when acting as a seat for hamza.

When hamza is the first consonant in a word, it is always written either above or below an ʾalif seat: - It is written above ʾalif (أ) when the following vowel is /a/ (أَ) or /u/ (أُ) - these are pronounced /ʔa/ and /ʔu/, respectively. - It is written below ʾalif (إ) when the following vowel is /i/ (إِ) - this is pronounced /ʔi/.

It is also common to omit a word-initial hamza symbol and only write the ʾalif seat.

Note: Weak Hamza (هَمْزَة الوَصْل, hamzat al-waṣl)

In certain situations, the [[TODO|glottal stop]] /ʔ/ at a word-initial position is pronounced only if the word is at the beginning of a sentence and it is otherwise dropped completely. Such a [[TODO|glottal stop]] /ʔ/ is known as a weak hamza (هَمْزَة الوَصْل, hamzat al-waṣl) and is indicated by an ʾalif seat without a hamza symbol. In vocalized texts, it is indicated by ٱ (an ʾalif with a waṣlah sign).

A medial hamza is written on the line as an unlinked letter when: - denoting /ʔa(ː)/ preceded by an ʾalif denoting the long vowel /aː/ - قِرَاءَة (qirā'a). - denoting /ʔa(ː)/ or /ʔu(ː)/ preceded by a wāw denoting the long vowel /uː/ or by a wāw without a subsequent vowel - مُرُوءَة (murūʾa), ضَوْءُهُ (ḍawʾuhu).

In all other situations, a medial hamza is written on one of the three seats. The seat is determined by the vowels surrounding the hamza with precedence according to the order /i(ː)/ > /u(ː)/ > /a(ː)/. - If there is an /i(ː)/ either preceding or following /ʔ/, then hamza takes yāʾ as a seat - سُئِلَ (suʾila), بِئْر (biʾr). - If there is no /i(ː)/ surrounding the /ʔ/ but there is /u(ː)/ either before or after it, then hamza takes wāw as a seat - سُؤَال (su'āl), رُؤُوس (ruʾūs). - If there is neither /i(ː)/ nor /u(ː)/ surrounding the /ʔ/, but there is /a(ː)/ either before or after it, then hamza takes ʾalif as a seat - سَأَلَ (saʾala), رَأْس (raʾs).

A final hamza is written on the line as an unlinked letter when preceded by any long vowel or any consonant - عِبْء (ʿibʾ), سَمَاء (samāʾ), هُدُوء (hudūʾ), شَيْء (shayʾ). It is written on a seat when preceded by a short vowel. The vowel determines which seat to take: - /a/ -> ʾalif, such as in قَرَأَ (qaraʾa); - /u/ -> wāw, such as in تَكَافُؤ (takāfuʾ) ; - /i/ -> yāʾ, such as in شَاطِئ (shāṭiʾ).

Note: ألِف مدَّة (ʾalif madda)

A special symbol (آ) known as ألِف مدَّة (ʾalif madda) is used to denote the combination /ʔaː/ of a [[TODO|glottal stop]] /ʔ/ followed by the long vowel /aː/.

docs.title: Gemination
docs.text:
Gemination or doubling of a consonant is indicated not by writing the letter for it twice but rather by placing a special diacritic ــّـ called شَدَّة (shaddah) on top of it.

Diacritic Name (Arabic Script) Name (Romanized) Meaning ــّـ شَدَّة shaddah Doubling of the consonant.

A shaddah may be combined with another diacritic for indicating a short vowel.

docs.title: Ligatures
docs.text:
Ligatures are quire common in written Arabic. Although there are many optional ligatures, the ligature between ل and ا is compulsory.

Final Medial Initial Isolated Letters IPA ﻼ ﻼ ﻻ‎ ﻻ‎ ل + ا /la:/

docs.title: Consonants
docs.text:
Arabic has 28 [[TODO|consonant]] [[TODO|phonemes]].

Consonant Phonemes of Modern Standard Arabic Labial Dental Denti-Alveolar Post-Alveolar / Palatal Velar Uvular Pharyngeal Glottal Plain Emphatic Nasal m م n ن Plosive Voiceless t ت tˤ ط k ك q ق ʔ ء Voiced b ب d د dˤ ض d͡ʒ ج Fricative Voiceless f ف θ ث s س sˤ ص ʃ ش x خ ħ ح h هـ Voiced ð ذ z ز ðˤ ظ ɣ غ ʕ ع Trill r ر Approximant l ل j ي w و

The consonants /sˤ/, /dˤ/, /tˤ/, /ðˤ/ are known as emphatic consonants.

docs.title: Vowels
docs.text:
Arabic has only six [[TODO|vowel]] [[TODO|phonemes]] and they manifest as three pairs of long and short sounds.

Arabic Vowels Front Central Back Close /i(ː)/ /u(ː)/ Mid Open /a(ː)/

The [[TODO|phoneme]] /a/ is realized as [æ] when preceded by most consonants: - the [[TODO|labial]] [[TODO|consonants]] /m/, /b/ and /f/; - the non-emphatic [[TODO|coronal consonants]] /θ/, /ð/, /n/, /t/, /d/, /s/, /z/, /l/, /ʃ/ and /d͡ʒ/ (except /r/) - the [[TODO|glottal consonants]] /h/ and /ʔ/ - /j/, /k/ and /w/;

The [[TODO|phoneme]] /a/ is realized as [ɑ] when preceded by most consonants the emphatic consonants /sˤ/, /dˤ/, /tˤ/, /ðˤ/.

Note: Full Form and Pause Form

There are two styles of pronouncing final short vowels of words in Arabic:

  • When a word is pronounced in full form (وَصْل, waṣl), its final short vowel (if any) is always pronounced (e.g. كَتَبَ).
  • When a word is pronounced in pause form (وَقْف, waqf), its final short vowel (if any) is not pronounced (e.g. كَتَبْ).

Using full form for every word is rarely done. It is usually restricted to Quranic recitation, poetry, highly formal speeches and is also done when teaching the language. In formal contexts, pause form is used for the final word of each sentence and when there is a natural break for breathing. All other words are in full form. In informal contexts, pause form is used for pretty much all words.

Pause form also affects the pronunciation of tā' marbūṭa.

docs.title: Syllabification
docs.text:
[[TODO|Syllable]] structure in Arabic is fairly restricted because syllables are limited to one of five forms: - CV (light) - CVV (heavy) - CVC (heavy) - CVVC (super-heavy) - CVCC (super-heavy)

[[TODO|Syllables]] can never begin with a vowel. Even though it might sometimes seems like a [[TODO|syllable]] starts with a vowel, such [[TODO|syllables]] actually start with a [[TODO|glottal stop]].

docs.title: Accent
docs.text: Arabic has a [[TODO|stress accent]] system, similar to the one in English, where an accented (or stressed) syllable is pronounced slightly longer, more clearly and with a bit more volume. For the most part, stress is predictable and follows certain rules, although there are some variations between dialects. These rules are given below in order of decreasing precedence: - If the final syllable is CVVC or CVCC, then the stress falls on it (e.g. كِتَاب ki-TĀB, مُسْتَقِلّ mus-ta-QILL). - If the second-to-last syllable is CVV or CVC, then the stress falls on it (e.g. ) - If the second-to-last syllable is CV, then the stress falls on the third-to-last syllable (e.g. كَتَبَ KA-ta-ba).

docs.title: Adjectives (Bulgarian)
docs.text: The dictionary form is the indefinite masculine singular.

docs.title: Gender
docs.text: Every adjective has a form for each gender - masculine, feminine and neuter. The dictionary form is the indefinite masculine singular, while the indefinite feminine singular and the indefinite neuter singular are built from the dictionary form in a fairly regular manner by attaching different endings. There are no stress shifts but one should beware changes due to variable ya and mobile ъ and a few other rules. Luckily, these rules are always consistent between the feminine and neuter forms.

docs.title: Masculine Adjectives
docs.text:
The majority of adjectives have an indefinite masculine singular which ends in a consonant. This is known as a simple form or unaugmented form.

Example Masculine Singular бял (white) бо̀лен (sick) ба̀вен (slow) висо̀к (tall, high) глѝнен (clay) голя̀м (big) добъ̀р (good) дъ̀лъг (long) дрѐбен (tiny) желѐзен (iron) жълт (yellow) зелѐн (green) кро̀тък (calm) криста̀лен (crystal) лѐден (icy) мѝрен (peaceful) мра̀чен (dark) нов (new) о̀гнен (firy) пъ̀лен (full) ро̀зов (pink) снѐжен (snowy) щастлѝв (happy) червѐн (red)

Some adjectives have a masciline form ending in -и. This is known as an augmented form.

Example Masculine Singilar бра̀тски (brotherly) бъ̀лгарски (bulgarian) вра̀жески (hostile) го̀рски (related to forest) гра̀дски (of the city) дѐтски (related to child) ко̀зи (related to goat) о̀вчи (related to sheep) прия̀телски (friendly) ру̀ски (russian)

Some adjectives have both an unaugmented form ending in a consonant as well as an augmented form ending in -и. They are mostly equivalent, but the latter is uncommon in everyday speech.

Example Masculine Singular (Unaugmented) Masculine Singular (Augmented) го̀рен (upper) го̀рни (upper) до̀лен (lower) до̀лни (lower) чѐрен (black) чѐрни (black)

docs.title: Feminine Adjectives
docs.text:
Most adjectives build the feminine singular by appending -а to the masculine form. This is always done with the unaugmented masculine form if it exists. Otherwise, this is done after removing the -и from the augmented form.

  • One should beware changes due to variable ya and mobile ъ.
  • Most adjectives whose masculine singular ends in an unstressed ⟨ен⟩ drop the ⟨е⟩ in the feminine form, but many do not.
  • The vast majority of adjectives whose masculine singular ends in the suffix -ен preceded by ⟨а⟩, ⟨ъ⟩, ⟨о⟩, ⟨у⟩, ⟨е⟩ or ⟨и⟩ replace the ⟨е⟩ from the suffix with ⟨й⟩, but some retain it.
  • Adjective whose masculine singular ends in one of the suffixes -ъв, -ък, -ъл or -ър drop the ⟨ъ⟩ from the suffix.

docs.title: Number
docs.text:
Adjectives also have a plural form which is used with plural nouns regardless of their gender.

The plural is built by appending -и to the unaugmented masculine singular if it exists. Otherwise, the plural form is identical to the augmented masculine singular.

  • One should beware changes due to variable ya and mobile ъ.

docs.title: Definite Article (Bulgarian)
docs.text:
The definite article is used to indicate that a word refers to something which is unique or was previously mentioned. It is attached to the end of a word and takes one of the following forms depending on the word's type, gender, number, etymology and syntactic role: -а, -ът, -я, -ят, -та, -то, -те.

Info: Short and Full Article

The definite articles -а and -я are known as short article (кратък член), while -ът and -ят are known as full article (пълен член). They come in the pairs -а, -ът and -я, -ят and are only used with masculine singular forms. Whether a word takes a short article or a full article is determined by its syntactic role.

Important: Pronunciation of the Short and Full Articles

The articles -а and -ът are both pronounced [ɤ] when stressed and [ɐ] otherwise.

The articles -я and -ят are both pronounced [jɤ] when stressed [jɐ] otherwise.

Pronouncing the final -т in a full article is only done when the speaker explicitly wants to put additional emphasis on it.

docs.title: Nouns
docs.text: Nouns can take any one of the forms -а, -ът, -я, -ят, -та, -то, -те.

docs.title: Masculine Nouns
docs.text:
All masculine singular nouns ending in an etymologically non-palatalized consonant build the definite singular form by appending -а, -ът to the indefinite singular.

  • Pollysyllabic masculine nouns do not experience a stress shift, but monosyllabic ones may.
  • One should beware changes due to variable ya and movable ъ.
  • Nouns ending in the suffix -зъм drop the ⟨ъ⟩ when the definite article is attached.

All masculine singular nouns ending in -й form the definite singular by replacing -й with -я, -ят.

Example: Masculine Singular Nouns Ending in -й Indefinite Singular Definite Singular (Short Article) Definite Singular (Full Article) Notes бой (beating) бо̀я (the beating) бо̀ят (the beating гей (gay) гѐя (the gay) гѐят (the gay) край (end) кра̀я (the end) кра̀ят (the end) сла̀вей сла̀вея сла̀веят слой (layer) сло̀я (the layer) сло̀ят (the layer)

All masculine singular nouns ending in -а or -я form the definite singular by appending the article -та. There are no stress shifts.

Example: Masculine Singular Nouns with Definite Article -та Indefinite Singular Definite Singular баща̀ (father) баща̀та (the father) бояджѝя (painter) бояджѝята (the painter) колѐга (colleague) колѐгата (the colleague) слуга̀ (servant) слуга̀та (the servant) съдия̀ (judge) съдия̀та (the judge)

All masculine singular nouns ending in -о or -е form the definite singular by appending the article -то. There are no stress shifts.

Example: Masculine Singular Nouns with Definite Article -то Indefinite Singular Definite Singular аташѐ аташѐто ву̀йчо (uncle, brother of the mother) ву̀йчото (the uncle) дя̀до (grandfather, old man) дя̀дото (the grandfather, the old man) чѝчо (uncle, brother of the father) чѝчото (the uncle)

docs.title: Feminine Nouns
docs.text:
All feminine singular nouns form the definite singular by appending the article -та. Those which end in -а or -я do not experience a stress shift, while all others shift the stress to the definite article. When the stress shifts, one should beware changes due to variable ya.

docs.title: Neuter Nouns
docs.text:
All neuter singular nouns form the definite singular by appending the article -то. There are no stress shifts.

docs.title: Plural Nouns
docs.text:
All plural nouns ending in -е or -и form the definite by appending the article -те. There are no stress shifts.

docs.title: Adjectives
docs.text:
Adjectives use the following articles depending on gender and number.

Masculine Singular Feminine Singular Neuter Singular Plural -я, -ят -та -то -те

Adjectives do not experience additional stress shifts when taking the definite article. For the feminine singular, neuter singular and plural, the definite article is appended directly to the corresponding indefinite form. However, masculine singular adjectives are more complicated:

  • If the adjective has only an augmented form, then the article is appended directly to it.
  • If the adjective has an unaugmented form, then this form is augmented by appending ⟨и⟩ and the definite article is then appended to this form.
  • One should beware changes due to variable ya and mobile ъ.
  • Most masculine singular adjectives ending in an unstressed -ен drop the ⟨е⟩ when the article is attached, but many do not.
  • The vast majority of masculine singular adjectives ending in the suffix -ен preceded by ⟨а⟩, ⟨ъ⟩, ⟨о⟩, ⟨у⟩, ⟨е⟩ or ⟨и⟩ replace the ⟨е⟩ from the suffix with ⟨й⟩, but some retain it.
  • Masculine singular adjectives ending in one of the suffixes -ъв, -ък, -ъл or -ър drop the ⟨ъ⟩ from the suffix.
Example: Definite Forms of Masculine Singular Adjectives Masculine Singular Definite Masculine Singular (Short Article) Definite Masculine Singular (Full Article) Notes азо̀тен (of nitrogen) азо̀тния азо̀тният The unstressed ⟨е⟩ in the suffix -ен is dropped. ба̀вен (slow) ба̀вния ба̀вният The unstressed ⟨е⟩ in the suffix -ен is dropped. An ⟨и⟩ is attached before the article since the unaugmented form is used. бѐден (poor) бѐдния бѐдният The unstressed ⟨е⟩ in the suffix -ен is dropped. An ⟨и⟩ is attached before the article since the unaugmented form is used. безу̀мен (mindless) безу̀мния безу̀мният The unstressed ⟨е⟩ in the suffix -ен is dropped. An ⟨и⟩ is attached before the article since the unaugmented form must be used. гра̀дски (urban) гра̀дския гра̀дският The article is attached directly, since there is only an augmented form. гро̀зен (ugly) гро̀зния гро̀зният An ⟨и⟩ is attached before the article since the unaugmented form must be used. добъ̀р (good) добрѝя добрѝят The ⟨ъ⟩ from the suffix ⟨ър⟩ is dropped.
