docs.title: Optimization Problems
docs.text:
We are often interested in finding extrema of a real scalar field under specific conditions.

Imagine we are tasked with the construction of a box with a lid which should be able to fit exactly \(1\) cubic meter of stuff. We want to minimize the cost and thus the amount of material used for the box. In other words, we want to find the dimensions of the box which require the least material. Suppose the amount of material is given by

\[f(x, y, z) = \underset{\text{front and back}}{2xy} + \underset{\text{sides}}{2yz} + \underset{\text{bottom and lid}}{2xz}.\]

We see that \(f\) has no extrema on its own. However, we also have another condition: the box should have a volume of \(1\) cubic meter. This gives us a constraint for the dimensions \(x, y, z\):

\[xyz = 1\]

We are now looking for the dimensions \(x, y, z\) with \(xyz = 1\) for which \(f(x, y, z)\) is minimal. Mathematically, we are no longer searching for the extrema of \(f\) but rather of \(f\)'s restriction on \(\Omega = \{(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}_{\gt 0}^3 \mid xyz = 1\}\). It turns out that \(f\vert_{\Omega}\) does have extrema.

Definition: Optimization Problem

An optimization problem \((f, \Omega_{\text{ad}})\) consists of an objective function which is a real scalar field \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) and a set \(\Omega_{\text{ad}} \subseteq \mathcal{D}\) of admissible values.

Definition: Equality Constraint

An equality constraint is a real vector function \(g: \mathcal{D}_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(g(\boldsymbol{p}) = 0\) for all \(\boldsymbol{p} \in \Omega_{\text{ad}}\).

Example: \(f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2\) with \(-x^2 + y = -3\)

Consider the optimization problem \((f, \Omega_{\text{ad}})\) consisting of the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2\]

and the following admissible values:

\[\Omega_{\text{ad}} = \{ (x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid -x^2 + y = -3\}\]

The real scalar field \(g: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[g(x, y) = -x^2 + y + 3\]

is an equality constraint.

In fact, we could have written \(\Omega_{\text{ad}}\) as follows:

\[\Omega_{\text{ad}} = \{ (x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid g(x, y) = 0 \}\]

Definition: Local Solution

We say that \(\boldsymbol{p} \in \Omega_{\text{ad}}\) is a local solution of \((f, \Omega_{\text{ad}})\) if the restriction \(f\vert_{\Omega_{\text{ad}}}\) has a local extremum at \(\boldsymbol{p}\).

Definition: Global Solution

We say that \(\boldsymbol{p} \in \Omega_{\text{ad}}\) is a global solution of \((f, \Omega_{\text{ad}})\) if the restriction \(f\vert_{\Omega_{\text{ad}}}\) has a global extremum at \(\boldsymbol{p}\).

In the vast majority of cases, we are interested in only one type of local extrema: either local minima or local maxima.

Example: \(f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2\) with \(-x^2 + y + 3 = 0\)

Consider the optimization problem \((f, \Omega_{\text{ad}})\) consisting of the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2\]

and the following admissible values:

\[\Omega_{\text{ad}} = \{ (x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid -x^2 + y + 3 = 0\}\]

We have \((x, y) \in \Omega_{\text{ad}}\) if and only if \(y = x^2 - 3\). Therefore:

\[f|_{\Omega_{\text{ad}}}(x, y) = x^2 + (x^2 - 3)^2\]

Let \(\tilde{f}: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be the real function defined as follows:

\[\tilde{f}(x) = x^2 + (x^2 - 3)^2\]

We see that \(f|_{\Omega_{\text{ad}}}\) has a local extremum at \((x, y)\) if and only if \(\tilde{f}\) has a local extremum at \(x\). The derivative of \(\tilde{f}\) is the following:

\[\tilde{f}'(x) = 4x^3 - 10x\]

This is \(0\) at the following points:

\[x_1 = -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2} \qquad x_2 = 0 \qquad x_3 = \frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}\]

The second derivative of \(\tilde{f}\) is the following:

\[\tilde{f}''(x) = 12x^2 - 10\]

We have:

\[\tilde{f}''(x_1) = 20 \gt 0 \qquad \tilde{f}''(x_2) = -10 \lt 0 \qquad \tilde{f}''(x_3) = 20 \gt 0\]

Therefore, \(\tilde{f}\) has local minima at \(x_1\) and \(x_3\) and a local maximum at \(x_2\). This implies that \(f|_{\Omega_{\text{ad}}}(x, y)\) has local minima at \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}\right)\) and \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}\right)\) and a local maximum at \((0, -3)\).

If we are interested at the local minima, then we would say that \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}\right)\) and \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}\right)\) are the solutions and if we are interested at the local maxima, then the solution would be \((0, -3)\).

docs.title: Lagrange Multipliers
docs.text:
The method of Lagrange multipliers allows us to find possible local solutions to an optimization problem specified by an equality constraint.

Definition: Lagrangian Function

Let \((f, \Omega_{ ext{ad}})\) be an optimization problem, where \(f: \mathcal{D}_f \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) is a real scalar field and \(\Omega_{ ext{ad}}\) can be specified via an equality constraint \(g: \mathcal{D}_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}^m\) with \(m \lt n\):

\[\Omega_{ ext{ad}} = \{ oldsymbol{x} \in \mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g \mid g( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{0} \}\]

The Lagrangian function is the real scalar field \(\mathcal{L}: (\mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g) imes \mathbb{R}^m o \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) = f( oldsymbol{x}) + oldsymbol{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}} g( oldsymbol{x})\]

for all \( oldsymbol{x} \in \mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g\) and all \( oldsymbol{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}^m\).

Notation

If we denote \( oldsymbol{\lambda} = egin{bmatrix}\lambda_1 & \cdots & \lambda_m\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}}\), we also write \(\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, \lambda_1, \dotsc, \lambda_m)\).

Theorem: First-Order Necessary Optimality Condition for Optimization Problems

Let \((f, \Omega_{ ext{ad}})\) be an optimization problem, where \(f: \mathcal{D}_f \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) is a real scalar field and \(\Omega_{ ext{ad}}\) can be specified via an equality constraint \(g: \mathcal{D}_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}^m\) with \(m \lt n\):

\[\Omega_{ ext{ad}} = \{ oldsymbol{x} \in \mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g \mid g( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{0} \}\]

If \(f\vert_{\Omega_{ ext{ad}}}\) has a local extremum at \( oldsymbol{p} \in \Omega_{ ext{ad}}\) and \(f\) and the component functions \(g_1, \dotsc, g_m\) are continuously partially differentiable on an open neighborhood of \( oldsymbol{p}\) such that the gradients \( abla g_1 ( oldsymbol{p}), \dotsc, abla g_m ( oldsymbol{p})\) are linearly independent, then there exist \( ilde{\lambda}_1, \dotsc, ilde{\lambda}_m \in \mathbb{R}\) such that

\[ abla f( oldsymbol{p}) + ilde{\lambda}_1 abla g_1 ( oldsymbol{p}) + \cdots + ilde{\lambda}_m abla g_m ( oldsymbol{p}) = oldsymbol{0}.\]

Alternatively, using the Lagrangian function: If \(f\vert_{\Omega_{ ext{ad}}}\) has a local extremum at \( oldsymbol{p} \in \Omega_{ ext{ad}}\) and \(f\) and \(g\) are continuously partially differentiable on an open neighborhood of \( oldsymbol{p}\) such that the Jacobian matrix \(J_g( oldsymbol{p})\) has rank \(m\), then there exists some \( oldsymbol{ ilde{\lambda}} = egin{bmatrix} ilde{\lambda}_1, \dotsc, ilde{\lambda}_m \end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) such that the gradient of the Lagrangian function is zero at \(( oldsymbol{p}, oldsymbol{ ilde{\lambda}})\):

\[ abla \mathcal{L} ( oldsymbol{p}, oldsymbol{ ilde{\lambda}}) = oldsymbol{0}\]

Definition: Lagrange Multipliers

We call \( ilde{\lambda}_1, \dotsc, ilde{\lambda}_m\) Lagrange multipliers.

Notation

An alternative convention is sometimes used, where the Lagrange multipliers are defined as \(- ilde{\lambda}_1, \dotsc, - ilde{\lambda}_m\).

Proof

TODO

This theorem gives us a way to find solution candidates for optimization problems by solving the system

\[ egin{cases} abla f( oldsymbol{x}) + \lambda_1 abla g_1 ( oldsymbol{x}) + \cdots + \lambda_m abla g_m ( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{0} \ g_1( oldsymbol{x}) = 0 \ \vdots \ g_m( oldsymbol{x}) = 0\end{cases}\]

for \( oldsymbol{x}\) and \(\lambda_1, \dotsc, \lambda_m\).

Notation

We can also write this system using the Lagrangian function. The condition \( abla \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{p})\)

\[ abla \mathcal{L} ( oldsymbol{p}, oldsymbol{ ilde{\lambda}}) = oldsymbol{0}\]

is equivalent to the following:

\[ egin{cases} \partial_{x_1} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{p}, oldsymbol{ ilde{\lambda}}) & = & 0 \ & \vdots & \ \partial_{x_n} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{p}, oldsymbol{ ilde{\lambda}}) & = & 0 \ \partial_{\lambda_1} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{p}, oldsymbol{ ilde{\lambda}}) & = & 0 \ & \vdots & \ \partial_{\lambda_m} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{p}, oldsymbol{ ilde{\lambda}}) & = & 0\end{cases}\]

Therefore, the solutions to the system

\[ egin{cases} \partial_{x_1} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) & = & 0 \ & \vdots & \ \partial_{x_n} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) & = & 0 \ \partial_{\lambda_1} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) & = & 0 \ & \vdots & \ \partial_{\lambda_m} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) & = & 0\end{cases}\]

are candidates for solutions of the optimization problem. Since \(\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) = f( oldsymbol{x}) + oldsymbol{\lambda}^{\mathsf{T}} g( oldsymbol{x})\) can be expressed as

\[\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) = f( oldsymbol{x}) + \lambda_1 g_1( oldsymbol{x}) + \cdots + \lambda_m g_m( oldsymbol{x}),\]

the first \(n\) equations are equivalent to the following:

\[ egin{cases}\lambda_1 abla g_1( oldsymbol{x}) = 0 \ \vdots \ \lambda_m abla g_m( oldsymbol{x}) = 0\end{cases}\]

This is often written as

\[ abla_{ oldsymbol{x}} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) = oldsymbol{0}\]

and we get:

\[ egin{cases} abla_{ oldsymbol{x}} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) & = & oldsymbol{0} \ \partial_{\lambda_1} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) & = & 0 \ & \vdots & \ \partial_{\lambda_m} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{x}, oldsymbol{\lambda}) & = & 0\end{cases}\] Example: \(f(x, y) = x^3 y^3\) under \(g(x, y) = x^2 + 2y^2 - 1 = 0\)

Consider the optimization problem \((f, \Omega_{ ext{ad}})\) consisting of the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 o \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[f(x, y) = x^3 y^3\]

and the admissible values due to the the equality constraint \(g: \mathbb{R}^2 o \mathbb{R}\):

\[g(x, y) = x^2 + 2y^2 - 1\] \[\Omega_{ ext{ad}} = \{ (x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \mid x^2 + 2y^2 - 1 = 0\}\]

Both \(f\) and \(g\) are continuously partially differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). For the Jacobian matrix \(J_g(x, y)\), we have:

\[J_g(x, y) = egin{bmatrix}2x & 4y\end{bmatrix}\]

Its rank is \(0 \lt 1\) if and only if \((x,y) = (0,0)\). However, \((0,0) otin \Omega_{ ext{ad}}\), since \(g(0,0) = 0^2 + 2\cdot 0^2 - 1 = -1 e 0\). Therefore, the Jacobian matrix has full rank for all \((x, y) \in \Omega_{ ext{ad}}\). We can thus use the theorem to find solution candidates.

We have Lagrangian function

\[\mathcal{L}(x, y, \lambda) = f(x, y) + \lambda g(x,y) = x^3y^3 + \lambda (x^2 + 2y^2 -1)\]

with the following gradient:

\[ abla \mathcal{L}(x, y, \lambda) = egin{bmatrix}3x^2y^3 + 2\lambda x \ 3x^3y^2 + 4\lambda y \ x^2 + 2y^2 - 1\end{bmatrix}\]

Therefore, we want to solve the following system:

\[ egin{cases}3x^2y^3 + 2\lambda x = 0 \ 3x^3y^2 + 4\lambda y = 0 \ x^2 + 2y^2 - 1 = 0\end{cases}\]

We multiply the first equation by \(x\), the second by \(y\) and examine the difference:

\[2 \lambda (x^2 - 2y^2) = 0\]

We thus have \(\lambda = 0\) or \(x = -\sqrt{2}y\) or \(x = +\sqrt{2}y\).

If \(\lambda = 0\), we get \(3x^2y^3 = 0\) and so \(x\) or \(y\) must also be zero. For \(x = 0\), we get the following solutions by plugging \(x\) into the third equation:

\[(\lambda_1, x_1, y_1) = \left(0, 0, - rac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ight) \qquad (\lambda_2, x_2, y_2) = \left(0, 0, + rac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ight)\]

For \(y = 0\), we get the following solutions by plugging \(x\) into the third equation:

\[(\lambda_3, x_3, y_3) = \left(0, -1, 0 ight) \qquad (\lambda_4, x_4, y_4) = \left(0, 1, 0 ight)\]

If \(\lambda e 0\), and \(x = -\sqrt{2}y\), plugging this into the third equation gives \((-\sqrt{2}y)^2 + 2y^2 - 1 = 0 \implies 4y^2 = 1 \implies y = \pm rac{1}{2}\).

For \(y = rac{1}{2}\), we get \(x = - rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\). We can find \(\lambda\) by substituting into the first equation (\(2\lambda x = -3x^2y^3 \implies \lambda = - rac{3}{2}xy^3\)):

\[\lambda = - rac{3}{2}\left(- rac{\sqrt{2}}{2} ight)\left( rac{1}{2} ight)^3 = rac{3\sqrt{2}}{32}\]

For \(y = - rac{1}{2}\), we get \(x = rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\). Finding \(\lambda\):

\[\lambda = - rac{3}{2}\left( rac{\sqrt{2}}{2} ight)\left(- rac{1}{2} ight)^3 = rac{3\sqrt{2}}{32}\]

This yields the following solutions:

\[(\lambda_5, x_5, y_5) = \left( rac{3\sqrt{2}}{32}, - rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, rac{1}{2} ight) \qquad (\lambda_6, x_6, y_6) = \left( rac{3\sqrt{2}}{32}, rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, - rac{1}{2} ight)\]

If \(\lambda e 0\), and \(x = +\sqrt{2}y\), plugging this into the third equation similarly gives \(4y^2 = 1 \implies y = \pm rac{1}{2}\).

For \(y = rac{1}{2}\), we get \(x = rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\). Finding \(\lambda\):

\[\lambda = - rac{3}{2}\left( rac{\sqrt{2}}{2} ight)\left( rac{1}{2} ight)^3 = - rac{3\sqrt{2}}{32}\]

For \(y = - rac{1}{2}\), we get \(x = - rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\). Finding \(\lambda\):

\[\lambda = - rac{3}{2}\left(- rac{\sqrt{2}}{2} ight)\left(- rac{1}{2} ight)^3 = - rac{3\sqrt{2}}{32}\]

This yields the following solutions:

\[(\lambda_7, x_7, y_7) = \left(- rac{3\sqrt{2}}{32}, rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, rac{1}{2} ight) \qquad (\lambda_8, x_8, y_8) = \left(- rac{3\sqrt{2}}{32}, - rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, - rac{1}{2} ight)\]

Our candidates are thus the following:

\[ egin{aligned}(x_1, y_1) &= \left(0, - rac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ight) & (x_2, y_2) & = \left(0, rac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ight) \(x_3, y_3) & = \left(-1, 0 ight) & (x_4, y_4) &= \left(1, 0 ight) \ (x_5, y_5) & = \left(- rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, rac{1}{2} ight) & (x_6, y_6) &= \left( rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, - rac{1}{2} ight) \ (x_7, y_7) &= \left( rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, rac{1}{2} ight) & (x_8, y_8) &= \left(- rac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, - rac{1}{2} ight)\end{aligned}\]

However, these are not guaranteed to be solutions to the optimization problem without further investigation.

Example: \(f(x, y, z) = x^2\) under \(g_1(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 1 = 0\) and \(g_2 (x, y, z) = x - z = 0\)

Consider the optimization problem \((f, \Omega_{ ext{ad}})\) consisting of the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^3 o \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[f(x, y, z) = x^2\]

and the admissible values due to the the equality constraints \(g_1: \mathbb{R}^3 o \mathbb{R}\) and \(g_2: \mathbb{R}^3 o \mathbb{R}\):

\[g_1(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 1 \qquad g_2(x, y, z) = x - z\] \[\Omega_{ ext{ad}} = \{ (x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid g_1(x, y, z) = g_2(x, y, z) = 0\}\]

Both \(f\), \(g_1\), and \(g_2\) are continuously partially differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^3\). For the Jacobian matrix \(J_g(x, y, z)\) where \(g = (g_1, g_2)\), we have:

\[J_g(x, y, z) = egin{bmatrix}2x & 2y & 2z \ 1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]

The rank of \(J_g(x, y, z)\) is strictly less than 2 if and only if its rows are linearly dependent, which occurs when \(y = 0\) and \(x = -z\). We must check if any such points exist in \(\Omega_{ ext{ad}}\). If \(x = -z\), the second constraint \(g_2(x, y, z) = x - z = 0\) forces \(x = 0\) and \(z = 0\). Plugging \((0, 0, 0)\) into the first constraint yields \(g_1(0,0,0) = -1 e 0\). Therefore, no point where the rank drops exists in \(\Omega_{ ext{ad}}\), meaning the Jacobian matrix has full rank for all \((x, y, z) \in \Omega_{ ext{ad}}\). We can thus use the theorem to find solution candidates.

We have Lagrangian function

\[\mathcal{L}(x, y, z, \lambda_1, \lambda_2) = f(x, y, z) + \lambda_1 g_1(x,y,z) + \lambda_2 g_2(x,y,z) = x^2 + \lambda_1 (x^2 + y^2 + z^2 -1) + \lambda_2 (x - z)\]

with the following gradient:

\[ abla \mathcal{L}(x, y, z, \lambda_1, \lambda_2) = egin{bmatrix}2x + 2\lambda_1 x + \lambda_2 \ 2\lambda_1 y \ 2\lambda_1 z - \lambda_2 \ x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 1 \ x - z\end{bmatrix}\]

Therefore, we want to solve the following system:

\[ egin{cases}2x + 2\lambda_1 x + \lambda_2 = 0 \ 2\lambda_1 y = 0 \ 2\lambda_1 z - \lambda_2 = 0 \ x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 1 = 0 \ x - z = 0\end{cases}\]

From the second equation, we have \(\lambda_1 = 0\) or \(y = 0\).

If \(\lambda_1 = 0\), we get \(-\lambda_2 = 0 \implies \lambda_2 = 0\) from the third equation. Substituting these into the first equation yields \(2x = 0 \implies x = 0\). From the fifth equation, we get \(x - z = 0 \implies z = 0\). For \(x = 0\) and \(z = 0\), we get the following solutions by plugging into the fourth equation (\(0^2 + y^2 + 0^2 - 1 = 0 \implies y = \pm 1\)):

\[(\lambda_{1,1}, \lambda_{2,1}, x_1, y_1, z_1) = \left(0, 0, 0, -1, 0 ight) \qquad (\lambda_{1,2}, \lambda_{2,2}, x_2, y_2, z_2) = \left(0, 0, 0, 1, 0 ight)\]

If \(y = 0\), we get \(x - z = 0 \implies z = x\) from the fifth equation. Plugging \(y=0\) and \(z=x\) into the fourth equation gives \(x^2 + 0^2 + x^2 - 1 = 0 \implies 2x^2 = 1 \implies x = \pm rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). Since \(z = x\), this means \(z = \pm rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) as well.

Adding the first and third equations gives \(2x + 2\lambda_1(x+z) = 0\). Substituting \(z=x\) yields \(2x + 4\lambda_1 x = 0 \implies 2x(1 + 2\lambda_1) = 0\). Since \(x e 0\), we have \(1 + 2\lambda_1 = 0 \implies \lambda_1 = - rac{1}{2}\).

For \(x = rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(z = rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), we find \(\lambda_2\) by substituting into the third equation (\(\lambda_2 = 2\lambda_1 z\)):

\[\lambda_2 = 2\left(- rac{1}{2} ight)\left( rac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ight) = - rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]

For \(x = - rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(z = - rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), finding \(\lambda_2\):

\[\lambda_2 = 2\left(- rac{1}{2} ight)\left(- rac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ight) = rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]

This yields the following solutions:

\[(\lambda_{1,3}, \lambda_{2,3}, x_3, y_3, z_3) = \left(- rac{1}{2}, - rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, 0, rac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ight) \qquad (\lambda_{1,4}, \lambda_{2,4}, x_4, y_4, z_4) = \left(- rac{1}{2}, rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, - rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, 0, - rac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ight)\]

Our candidates are thus the following:

\[ egin{aligned}(x_1, y_1, z_1) &= \left(0, -1, 0 ight) & (x_2, y_2, z_2) & = \left(0, 1, 0 ight) \(x_3, y_3, z_3) & = \left( rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, 0, rac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ight) & (x_4, y_4, z_4) &= \left(- rac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, 0, - rac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ight)\end{aligned}\]

However, these are not guaranteed to be solutions to the optimization problem without further investigation.

docs.title: Polar Coordinate Representations (Real Scalar Fields)
docs.text:
Definition: Polar Coordinate Representation

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \(\mathcal{T}: [0, \infty) \times (0, 2\uppi) \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathcal{D}\) be the coordinate transformation from polar coordinates:

\[\mathcal{T}(\rho, \varphi) = \begin{bmatrix} \rho \cos \varphi \\ \rho \sin \varphi \end{bmatrix}\]

The polar coordinate representation of \(f\) is the composition \(f \circ \mathcal{T}\).

docs.title: Real-Valued Functions of Multiple Real Variables
Real-Valued Functions of Multiple Real Variables
docs.text:
Definition: Real-Valued Function of Multiple Real Variables

A real-valued function of \(n\) real variables is a real-valued function whose domain is a subset of the real vector space \(\mathbb{R}^n\):

\[f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\] Example

The function \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[f(x_1, \dotsc, x_n) \overset{\text{def}}{=} \sqrt{x_1^2 + \cdots x_n^2}\]

is a real scalar field.

Example

Let \(\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) be an open ball centered at \(\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and with radius \(r \gt 0\) and let \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) be any real matrix. The function \(f: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[f(\boldsymbol{x}) \overset{\text{def}}{=} \boldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}}A\boldsymbol{x}\]

is a real scalar field.

docs.title: Spherical Coordinate Representations (Real Scalar Fields)
docs.text:
Definition: Spherical Coordinate Representation

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \(\mathcal{T}: (0,+\infty) \times (0,\uppi) \times (0,2\uppi) \to \mathcal{D}\) be the coordinate transformation from spherical coordinates:

\[\mathcal{T}(r, \theta, \varphi) = \begin{bmatrix}r \sin \theta \cos \varphi \\ r \sin \theta \sin \varphi \\ r \cos \theta\end{bmatrix}\]

The spherical coordinate representation of \(f\) is the composition \(f \circ \mathcal{T}\).

docs.text:
Definition: Taylor Polynomial

TODO

Theorem: Taylor Polynomial via Partial Derivatives

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field.

If \(f\) is \(m\)-times totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}\), then its Taylor polynomial there is given by \(f\)'s partial derivatives as follows:

\[T( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x}) = f( oldsymbol{p}) + \sum_{k = 1}^m rac{1}{k!}\left(\sum_{i_1 = 1}^n\cdots \sum_{i_k = 1}^n \partial_{i_1}\cdots \partial_{i_k}f( oldsymbol{p}) \prod_{j = 1}^k (x_{i_j} - p_{i_j}) ight)\]

Tip

This formula can be rewritten using \(f\)'s gradient and Hessian matrix as follows:

\[T( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x}) = f( oldsymbol{p}) + abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}}( oldsymbol{x}- oldsymbol{p}) + rac{1}{2} ( oldsymbol{x}- oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{H}_f( oldsymbol{p})( oldsymbol{x}- oldsymbol{p}) + \sum_{k = 3}^m rac{1}{k!}\left(\sum_{i_1 = 1}^n\cdots \sum_{i_k = 1}^n \partial_{i_1}\cdots \partial_{i_k}f( oldsymbol{p}) \prod_{j = 1}^k (x_{i_j} - p_{i_j}) ight)\] Proof

Theorem: Lagrange Form of the Remainder

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \( oldsymbol{p}, oldsymbol{x} \in \mathcal{D}\).

If \(f\) is \((m+1)\)-times totally differentiable on an open set which contains \(L = \{ oldsymbol{p} + t( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}): t \in [0,1]\}\), then there exists some \( oldsymbol{\xi} \in \operatorname{int} L\) such that the remainder \(R_{m+1}( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x})\) of \(f\)'s \(m\)-th Taylor polynomial \(T_m( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x})\) is given by \(f\)'s partial derivatives as follows:

\[R_{m+1}( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x}) = rac{1}{(m+1)!} \left(\sum_{i_1 = 1}^n\cdots \sum_{i_{m+1} = 1}^n \partial_{i_1}\cdots \partial_{i_{m+1}}f( oldsymbol{\xi}) \prod_{j = 1}^{m+1} (x_{i_j} - p_{i_j}) ight),\] Proof

Theorem: Integral Form of the Remainder

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \( oldsymbol{p}, oldsymbol{x} \in \mathcal{D}\).

If \(f\) is \((m+1)\)-times continuously partially differentiable on an open set which contains \(L = \{ oldsymbol{p} + t( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}): t \in [0,1]\}\), then the remainder \(R_{m+1}( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x})\) of \(f\)'s \(m\)-th Taylor polynomial \(T_m( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x})\) is given by the following integral:

\[R_{m+1}( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x}) = rac{1}{m!}\int_0^1 (1-t)^m \left(\sum_{i_1 = 1}^n\cdots \sum_{i_{m+1} = 1}^n \partial_{x^{i_1}}\cdots \partial_{x^{i_{m+1}}}f( oldsymbol{p} + t( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})) \prod_{j = 1}^{m+1} (x^{i_j} - p^{i_j}) ight)\,\mathrm{d}t\] Proof

Theorem: Remainder and Bachmann-Landau Notation

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \mathcal{D}\).

If \(f\) is \(m\)-times totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\), then the remainder \(R_{m+1}( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x}) = f( oldsymbol{x}) - T_m( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x})\) of \(f\)'s \(m\)-th Taylor polynomial \(T_m( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x})\) is little o of \(|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||^m\) for \( oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}\):

\[R_{m+1}( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x}) = o(|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||^m) \qquad ext{for} \qquad oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}\]

If \(f\) is \((m+1)\)-times continuously partially differentiable on an open neighborhood of \( oldsymbol{p}\), then the remainder \(R_{m+1}( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x}) = f( oldsymbol{x}) - T_m( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x})\) of \(f\)'s \(m\)-th Taylor polynomial \(T_m( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x})\) is Big O of \(|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||^{m+1}\) for \( oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}\):

\[R_{m+1}( oldsymbol{p}; oldsymbol{x}) = O(|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||^{m+1}) \qquad ext{for} \qquad oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}\] Example: \(f(x, y) = x^3 \mathrm{e}^{y}\)

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 o \mathbb{R}\) defined as follows:

\[f\left(x, y ight) = x^3 \mathrm{e}^{y}\]

For its partial derivatives, we have:

\[\partial_{x}f(x, y) = 3x^2 \mathrm{e}^{y} \qquad \partial_{y}f(x, y) = x^3 \mathrm{e}^{y}\] \[\partial_{x}\partial_{x}f(x, y) = 6x \mathrm{e}^{y} \qquad \partial_{x}\partial_{y}f(x, y) = 3x^2 \mathrm{e}^{y} = \partial_{y}\partial_{x}f(x, y) \qquad \partial_{y}\partial_{y}f(x, y) = x^3 \mathrm{e}^{y}\]

Therefore:

\[f\left( egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight) = 1 \qquad abla f\left( egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight) = egin{bmatrix}3 \ 1\end{bmatrix} \qquad H_f\left( egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight) = egin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\]

We thus have:

\[ egin{aligned}f\left(x, y ight) & = T_2\left( egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix}; egin{bmatrix}x \ y\end{bmatrix} ight) + R_3\left( egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix}; egin{bmatrix}x \ y\end{bmatrix} ight) \ & = f\left( egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight) + abla f\left( egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight)^{\mathsf{T}}\left( egin{bmatrix}x \ y\end{bmatrix}- egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight) + rac{1}{2}\left( egin{bmatrix}x \ y\end{bmatrix}- egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight)^{\mathsf{T}} H_f\left( egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight) \left( egin{bmatrix}x \ y\end{bmatrix}- egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight) + R_3\left( egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix}; egin{bmatrix}x \ y\end{bmatrix} ight) \ & = f\left( egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight) + egin{bmatrix}3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\left( egin{bmatrix}x \ y\end{bmatrix}- egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight) + rac{1}{2}\left( egin{bmatrix}x \ y\end{bmatrix}- egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight)^{\mathsf{T}} egin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\left( egin{bmatrix}x \ y\end{bmatrix}- egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight) + O\left(\left\vert\left\vert egin{bmatrix}x \ y\end{bmatrix} - egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} ight\vert ight\vert^3 ight) \qquad ext{for} \qquad egin{bmatrix}x \ y\end{bmatrix} o egin{bmatrix}1 \ 0\end{bmatrix} \ & = f\left( egin{bmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{bmatrix} ight) + 3(x - 1) + y + 3(x - 1)^2 + 3(x - 1)y + rac{1}{2}y^2 + O\left(\left((x-1)^2 + y^2 ight)^{3/2} ight)\end{aligned}\] Proof

docs.title: Directional Differentiability (Real Scalar Fields)
docs.text:
Definition: Directional Differentiability of Real Scalar Fields

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field, let \( oldsymbol{d} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \mathcal{D}\) be such that \(0\) is an accumulation point of \(\{h \in \mathbb{R}\mid oldsymbol{p}+h oldsymbol{d} \in \mathcal{D}\}\).

We say that \(f\) is directionally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\) along \( oldsymbol{d}\) if the limit

\[\lim_{t o 0} rac{f( oldsymbol{p} + t \cdot oldsymbol{d} ) - f( oldsymbol{p})}{t}\]

exists. The value of this limit is known as \(f\)'s directional derivative at \( oldsymbol{p}\) along \( oldsymbol{d}\).

Notation

\[ rac{\partial f}{\partial oldsymbol{d}}( oldsymbol{p}) \qquad \partial_{ oldsymbol{d}}f( oldsymbol{p}) \qquad f_{ oldsymbol{d}}( oldsymbol{p}) \qquad D_{ oldsymbol{d}} f( oldsymbol{p})\]

Theorem: Total Differentiability \(\implies\) Directional Differentiability

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int}\mathcal{D}\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}\).

If \(f\) is totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\), then it is directionally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\) along each \( oldsymbol{r} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and its directional derivative of \(f\) along \( oldsymbol{r}\) is given by the dot product of \(f\)'s gradient and \( oldsymbol{r}\):

\[\partial_{ oldsymbol{r}}f( oldsymbol{p}) = abla f( oldsymbol{p}) \cdot oldsymbol{r}\] Example: \(f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x}\)

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x}\]

for some fixed real vector \( oldsymbol{a} = egin{bmatrix} a^1 & \cdots & a^n \end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}}\in \mathbb{R}^n\).

It is totally differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and its gradient is the following:

\[ abla f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{a}\]

Its directional derivatives are thus the following:

\[\partial_{ oldsymbol{r}} f( oldsymbol{x}) = abla f( oldsymbol{x}) \cdot oldsymbol{r} = oldsymbol{a} \cdot oldsymbol{r}\] Example: \(f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x}\)

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x}\]

for some real matrix \( oldsymbol{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n imes n}\).

It is totally differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and its gradient is the following:

\[ abla f( oldsymbol{x}) = ( oldsymbol{A} + oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}}) oldsymbol{x}\]

Therefore, its directional derivatives are as follows:

\[\partial_{ oldsymbol{r}} f( oldsymbol{x}) = abla f( oldsymbol{x}) \cdot oldsymbol{r} = abla f( oldsymbol{x})^{\mathsf{T}} \cdot oldsymbol{r} = oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}}( oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}} + oldsymbol{A}) oldsymbol{r}\] Example: Converse is False

TODO

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 o \mathbb{R}\) defined as follows:

\[f\left(x, y ight) = egin{cases} rac{x y^2}{x^2 + y^2} & ext{if } x e 0 ext{ and } y e 0 \ 0 & ext{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

For its directional derivatives at \( oldsymbol{0}\), we have:

\[ egin{aligned}\partial_{ oldsymbol{r}}f( oldsymbol{0}) & = \lim_{h o 0} rac{f( oldsymbol{0} + h oldsymbol{r}) - f( oldsymbol{0})}{h} \ & = \lim_{h o 0} rac{ rac{(hr_1)(hr_2)^2}{h^2 r_1^2 + h^2 r_2^2} - 0}{h} \ & = \lim_{h o 0} rac{ rac{h^3 r_1 r_2^2}{h^2(r_1^2 + r_2^2)}}{h} \ & = \lim_{h o 0} rac{ rac{h r_1 r_2^2}{r_1^2 + r_2^2}}{h} \ & = \lim_{h o 0} rac{hr_1 r_2^2}{h(r_1^2 + r_2^2)} \ & = \lim_{h o 0} rac{r_1 r_2^2}{r_1^2 + r_2^2} \ & = rac{r_1 r_2^2}{r_1^2 + r_2^2} \ & = f( oldsymbol{r})\end{aligned}\]

Therefore, all of \(f\)'s directional derivatives \( oldsymbol{0}\) exist. More specifically, its partial derivatives are the following:

\[ rac{\partial f}{\partial x}( oldsymbol{0}) = \partial_{ oldsymbol{e}_1} f( oldsymbol{0}) = f( oldsymbol{e}_1) = rac{1 \cdot 0^2}{1^2 + 0^2} = 0\] \[ rac{\partial f}{\partial y}( oldsymbol{0}) = \partial_{ oldsymbol{e}_2} f( oldsymbol{0}) = f( oldsymbol{e}_2) = rac{0 \cdot 1^2}{0^2 + 1^2} = 0\]

Therefore, \(f\)'s gradient is the following:

\[ abla f( oldsymbol{0}) = egin{bmatrix}\partial_{x}f( oldsymbol{0}) \ \partial_y f( oldsymbol{0})\end{bmatrix} = egin{bmatrix}0 \ 0\end{bmatrix} = oldsymbol{0}\]

The directional derivatives of \(f\) would then have to be given by

\[\partial_{ oldsymbol{r}}f( oldsymbol{0}) = abla f( oldsymbol{0}) \cdot oldsymbol{r} = oldsymbol{0} \cdot oldsymbol{r} = 0\]

but we just proved that \(f\)'s directional derivatives are given by the following:

\[\partial_{ oldsymbol{r}}f( oldsymbol{0}) = f( oldsymbol{r})\]

In general, this is not equal to \(0\) and so we have reached a contradiction. Therefore, \(f\) is not totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{0}\) even though all of its directional derivatives there exist.

To confirm this, we assume that \(f\) is totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{0}\). Therefore, there its gradient \( abla f( oldsymbol{0})\) exists and, since we just showed that \( abla f( oldsymbol{0}) = oldsymbol{0}\), we know that \(f( oldsymbol{0} + oldsymbol{h}) - f( oldsymbol{0}) - abla f( oldsymbol{0})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{h}\) is little o of \(|| oldsymbol{h}||\) for \( oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}\):

\[f( oldsymbol{0} + oldsymbol{h}) - f( oldsymbol{0}) - abla f( oldsymbol{0})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{h} = o(|| oldsymbol{h}||) \qquad ext{for} \qquad oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}\] \[f( oldsymbol{h}) - 0 - oldsymbol{0}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{h} = o(|| oldsymbol{h}||) \qquad ext{for} \qquad oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}\] \[f( oldsymbol{h}) = o(|| oldsymbol{h}||) \qquad ext{for} \qquad oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}\]

This implies the following limit:

\[\lim_{ oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}} rac{f( oldsymbol{h})}{|| oldsymbol{h}||} = 0\]

Let's examine the following real vector sequence \(( oldsymbol{h}_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}\):

\[ oldsymbol{h}_k = egin{bmatrix} rac{1}{k} \ rac{1}{k}\end{bmatrix}\]

Its limit for \(k o \infty\) is obviously \( oldsymbol{0}\). Furthermore, we have the following [limit](../../Real%20Functions/Limits%20(Real%20Functions.md):

\[ egin{aligned}\lim_{k o \infty} rac{f( oldsymbol{h}_k)}{|| oldsymbol{h}_k||} & = \lim_{k o \infty} rac{ rac{ rac{1}{k} \cdot rac{1}{k^2}}{ rac{1}{k^2} + rac{1}{k^2}}}{\sqrt{ rac{1}{k^2} + rac{1}{k^2}}} \ & = \lim_{k o \infty} rac{ rac{1/k^3}{2/k^2}}{\sqrt{2/k^2}} \ & = \lim_{k o \infty} rac{ rac{1}{2k}}{ rac{\sqrt{2}}{k}} \ & = \lim_{k o \infty} rac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \ & = rac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\end{aligned}\]

Since \( rac{\sqrt{2}}{4} e 0\), we know that \(\lim_{ oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}} rac{f( oldsymbol{h})}{|| oldsymbol{h}||} e 0\) and so we reached a contradiction. Therefore, \(f\) cannot be totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{0}\).

Proof

Since \(f\) is totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\), we have that \(f( oldsymbol{p} + oldsymbol{h}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{h}\) is little o of \(|| oldsymbol{h}||\) for \( oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}\):

\[f( oldsymbol{p} + oldsymbol{h}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{h} = o(|| oldsymbol{h}||) \qquad ext{for} \qquad oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}\]

This implies that

\[f( oldsymbol{p} + h oldsymbol{r}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}}(h oldsymbol{r}) = o(h|| oldsymbol{r}||) \qquad ext{for} \qquad h o 0\]

and so

\[f( oldsymbol{p} + h oldsymbol{r}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - h abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{r} = || oldsymbol{r}|| o(h) \qquad ext{for} \qquad h o 0\]

and

\[f( oldsymbol{p} + h oldsymbol{r}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - h abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{r} = o(h) \qquad ext{for} \qquad h o 0.\]

This implies the following:

\[\lim_{h o 0} rac{f( oldsymbol{p} + h oldsymbol{r}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - h abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{r}}{h} = 0\]

We have:

\[ egin{aligned}\partial_{ oldsymbol{r}} f( oldsymbol{p}) & = \lim_{h o 0} rac{f( oldsymbol{p} + h oldsymbol{r}) - f( oldsymbol{p})}{h} \ & = \lim_{h o 0} \left( rac{f( oldsymbol{p} + h oldsymbol{r}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - h abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{r}}{h} + rac{h abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{r}}{h} ight) \ & = \lim_{h o 0} rac{f( oldsymbol{p} + h oldsymbol{r}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - h abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{r}}{h} + \lim_{h o 0} rac{h abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{r}}{h} \ & = 0 + abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{r} \ & = abla f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{r} \ & = abla f( oldsymbol{p}) \cdot oldsymbol{r}\end{aligned}\]

docs.title: Gradient (Real Scalar Fields)
docs.text:
Definition: Gradient

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field, let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}\) and suppose that \(f\) is partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\).

The gradient of \(f\) at \( oldsymbol{p}\) is the vector whose components are \(f\)'s partial derivatives at \( oldsymbol{p}\):

\[ egin{bmatrix} \partial_1 f( oldsymbol{p}) \ \vdots \ \partial_n f( oldsymbol{p}) \end{bmatrix}\]

Notation

\[ abla f( oldsymbol{p}) \qquad \operatorname{grad} f( oldsymbol{p})\] Example: \(f(x, y) = x^2 y^3 + x\)

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 o \mathbb{R}\) defined as follows:

\[f\left(x, y ight) = x^2 y^3 + x\]

It is partially differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\):

\[ rac{\partial f}{\partial x} \left(x, y ight) = 2x y^3 + 1 \qquad rac{\partial f}{\partial y} \left(x, y ight) = 3 x^2 y^2\]

Its gradient is thus the following for all \( egin{bmatrix}x & y\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}} \in \mathbb{R}^2\):

\[ abla f(x,y) = egin{bmatrix} 2x y^3 + 1 \ 3 x^2 y^2\end{bmatrix}\] Example: \(f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x}\)

Let \( oldsymbol{a} = egin{bmatrix} a_1 & \cdots & a_n \end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}}\in \mathbb{R}^n\) be a real vector and consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) defined as follows:

\[f( oldsymbol{x}) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x} = a_1 x_1 + \cdots + a_n x_n\]

We see that \(f\) is partially differentiable at every \( oldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\):

\[\partial_1 f( oldsymbol{x}) = a_1 \qquad \cdots \qquad \partial_n f( oldsymbol{x}) = a_n\]

Therefore, \(f\)'s gradient is the following for each \( oldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\):

\[ abla f( oldsymbol{x}) = egin{bmatrix}a_1 \ \vdots \ a_n\end{bmatrix} = oldsymbol{a}\] Example: \(f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x}\)

Let \( oldsymbol{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n imes n}\) be a real matrix

\[ oldsymbol{A} = egin{bmatrix}A_{11} & \cdots & A_{1n} \ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ A_{n1} & \cdots & A_{nn}\end{bmatrix}\]

and consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) defined as follows:

\[f( oldsymbol{x}) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} = \sum_{i = 1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n x_i A_{ij} x_j\]

We see that \(f\) is partially differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). By applying the product rule, we get the following for each \(k \in \{1, \dotsc, n\}\):

\[ egin{aligned}\partial_k f(x_1, \dotsc, x_n) & = \partial_k \left(\sum_{i = 1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n x_i A_{ij} x_j ight) \ & = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n \partial_k (x_i A_{ij} x_j) \ & = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n (\partial_k x_i) A_{ij} x_j + x_i \partial_k (A_{ij} x_j) \ & = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n (\partial_k x_i) A_{ij} x_j + x_i A_{ij}(\partial_k x_j) \ & = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n (\partial_k x_i) A_{ij} x_j + \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n x_i A_{ij}(\partial_k x_j)\end{aligned}\]

We have \(\partial_k x_i = 1\) for \(i = k\) and \(\partial_k x_i = 0\) otherwise. Summing over \(i\) leaves only the one term where \(i = k\) and so the first sum collapses to the following:

\[\sum_{i = 1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n (\partial_k x_i) A_{ij} x_j = \sum_{j = 1}^n A_{kj} x_j\]

By the same token, \(\partial_k x_j = 1\) for \(j = k\) and \(\partial_k x_j = 0\) otherwise. Summing over \(j\) leaves only the one term where \(j = k\) and so the second sum collapses to the following:

\[\sum_{i = 1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n x_i A_{ij}(\partial_k x_j) = \sum_{i = 1}^n x_i A_{ik}\]

Together, we get:

\[\partial_k f(x_1, \dotsc, x_n) = \sum_{j = 1}^n A_{kj} x_j + \sum_{i = 1}^n x_i A_{ik}\]

Therefore, \(f\)'s gradient is given as follows for each \( oldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\):

\[ egin{aligned} abla f(x_1, \dotsc, x_n) & = egin{bmatrix} \sum_{j = 1}^n A_{1j} x_j + \sum_{i = 1}^n x_i A_{i1} \ \vdots \ \sum_{j = 1}^n A_{nj} x_j + \sum_{i = 1}^n x_i A_{in}\end{bmatrix} \ & = egin{bmatrix} \sum_{j = 1}^n A_{1j} x_j \ \vdots \ \sum_{j = 1}^n A_{nj} x_j\end{bmatrix} + egin{bmatrix}\sum_{i = 1}^n x_i A_{i1} \ \vdots \ \sum_{i = 1}^n x_i A_{in} \end{bmatrix} \ & = oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} + oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x} \ & = ( oldsymbol{A}+ oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}}) oldsymbol{x} \end{aligned}\]

Theorem: Gradient and Jacobian

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field, let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}\) and suppose that \(f\) is partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\).

The gradient of \(f\) at \( oldsymbol{p}\) is the transpose of \(f\)'s Jacobian matrix at \( oldsymbol{p}\):

\[ abla f( oldsymbol{p}) = (J_f( oldsymbol{p}))^{\mathsf{T}}\] Proof

Theorem: Total Differentiability of Real Scalar Fields

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}\).

Then \(f\) is totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\) if and only if the following limit involving a dot product with \(f\)'s gradient is zero:

\[\lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{f( oldsymbol{x}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - abla f( oldsymbol{p}) \cdot ( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} = 0,\] Example: \(f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x}\)

Let \( oldsymbol{a} = egin{bmatrix} a_1 & \cdots & a_n \end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}}\in \mathbb{R}^n\) be a real vector and consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) defined as follows:

\[f( oldsymbol{x}) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x} = a_1 x_1 + \cdots + a_n x_n\]

Its gradient is the following for all \( oldsymbol{p} \in \mathbb{R}^n\):

\[ abla f( oldsymbol{p}) = oldsymbol{a}\]

Now, for each \( oldsymbol{p} \in \mathbb{R}^n\), we have

\[ egin{aligned}\lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{f( oldsymbol{x}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - abla f( oldsymbol{x}) \cdot ( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{f( oldsymbol{x}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - oldsymbol{a} \cdot ( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{ oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{p} - oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}}( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{ oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}}( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}) - oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}}( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{0}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = 0\end{aligned}\]

Therefore, \(f\) is totally differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

Example: \(f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x}\)

Let \( oldsymbol{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n imes n}\) be a real matrix

\[ oldsymbol{A} = egin{bmatrix}A_{11} & \cdots & A_{1n} \ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ A_{n1} & \cdots & A_{nn}\end{bmatrix}\]

and consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) defined as follows:

\[f( oldsymbol{x}) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} = \sum_{i = 1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n x_i A_{ij} x_j\]

Its gradient is the following for all \( oldsymbol{p} \in \mathbb{R}^n\):

\[ abla f( oldsymbol{p}) = ( oldsymbol{A} + oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}}) oldsymbol{p}\]

Now, for each \( oldsymbol{p} \in \mathbb{R}^n\), we have:

\[ egin{aligned}\lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{f( oldsymbol{x}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) - abla f( oldsymbol{p}) \cdot ( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{ oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{p} - (( oldsymbol{A} + oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}}) oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}}( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{ oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{p} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}}( oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}} + A)( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{ oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{p} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} ( oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{p} + oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{ oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{p} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x} + oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{p} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} + oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{p}}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{ oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x} + oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{p} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x}}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{ oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} - ( oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} + ( oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x}}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{ oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{p} + oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{p} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x}}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{ oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} ( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}) - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} ( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{( oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} - oldsymbol{p}^{\mathsf{T}}) oldsymbol{A} ( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} \ & = \lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} ( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||}\end{aligned}\]

With the substitution \( oldsymbol{h} = oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p} = egin{bmatrix}h_1, \dotsc, h_n \end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}}\) we get:

\[\lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} ( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} = \lim_{ oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}} rac{ oldsymbol{h}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{h}}{|| oldsymbol{h}||}\]

The product \( oldsymbol{h}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{h}\) is given by the following:

\[ egin{aligned} oldsymbol{h}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{h} & = oldsymbol{h}^{\mathsf{T}}( oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{h}) = egin{bmatrix} h_1 & h_2 & \dots & h_n \end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix} \sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{1j} h_j \ \sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{2j} h_j \ \vdots \ \sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{nj} h_j \end{bmatrix} \ & = \sum_{i=1}^{n} h_i \left( \sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{ij} h_j ight) \ & = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{ij} h_i h_j\end{aligned}\]

We thus have:

\[| oldsymbol{h}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{h}| \leq \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} |A_{ij}| |h_i| |h_j|\]

From \(|| oldsymbol{h}|| = \sqrt{\sum_{k = 1}^n (h_k)^2}\), we know that

\[|h_k| \le || oldsymbol{h}||\]

for all \(k \in \{1,\dotsc,n\}\).

Therefore,

\[|h_i||h_j| \le || oldsymbol{h}||^2\]

for all \(i,j \in \{1,\dotsc,n\}\).

From this, we obtain the following:

\[| oldsymbol{h}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{h}| \leq \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} |A_{ij}| || oldsymbol{h}||^2 = || oldsymbol{h}||^2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} |A_{ij}|\]

The sum \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} |A_{ij}|\) is just a constant and so

\[| oldsymbol{h}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{h}| \leq C || oldsymbol{h}||^2\]

with \(C = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} |A_{ij}|\). Divide by \(|| oldsymbol{h}||\):

\[0 \le rac{| oldsymbol{h}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{h}|}{|| oldsymbol{h}||} \leq C || oldsymbol{h}||\]

We know that the limit of \(C || oldsymbol{h}||\) for \( oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}\) is zero. By the squeeze theorem we get:

\[\lim_{ oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}} rac{| oldsymbol{h}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{h}|}{|| oldsymbol{h}||} = 0,\]

i.e.

\[\lim_{ oldsymbol{x} o oldsymbol{p}} rac{( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} ( oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p})}{|| oldsymbol{x} - oldsymbol{p}||} = 0.\]

Therefore, \(f\) is totally differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

Theorem: Gradient of Linear Combination

Let \(f: \mathcal{D}_f \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) and \(g: \mathcal{D}_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be real scalar fields and let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} (\mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g)\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g\).

If \(f\) and \(g\) are partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\), then so is \(\lambda f + \mu g\) for all \(\lambda, \mu \in \mathbb{R}\) and its gradient is given by the gradients of \(f\) and \(g\) as follows:

\[ abla (\lambda f + \mu g)( oldsymbol{p}) = \lambda abla f( oldsymbol{p}) + \mu abla g( oldsymbol{p})\] Proof

Theorem: Product Rule with Gradients

Let \(f: \mathcal{D}_f \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) and \(g: \mathcal{D}_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be real scalar fields and let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} (\mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g)\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g\).

If \(f\) and \(g\) are partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\), then so is \(fg\) and its gradient is given by the gradients of \(f\) and \(g\) as follows:

\[ abla(fg)( oldsymbol{p}) = g( oldsymbol{p}) abla f( oldsymbol{p}) + f( oldsymbol{p}) abla g( oldsymbol{p})\] Proof

Since \(f\) and \(g\) are both partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\), we know that their partial derivatives \(\partial_k f( oldsymbol{p})\) and \(\partial_k g( oldsymbol{p})\) exist for all \(k \in \{1, \dotsc, n\}\). We apply the product rule:

\[\partial_k (fg)( oldsymbol{p}) = (\partial_k f)( oldsymbol{p})g( oldsymbol{p}) + f( oldsymbol{p})(\partial_k g)( oldsymbol{p}) = g( oldsymbol{p}) \partial_k f( oldsymbol{p}) + f( oldsymbol{p})\partial_k g( oldsymbol{p})\]

Therefore, the gradient of \(fg\) is the following:

\[ abla (fg)( oldsymbol{p}) = egin{bmatrix} g( oldsymbol{p}) \partial_1 f( oldsymbol{p}) + f( oldsymbol{p})\partial_1 g( oldsymbol{p}) \ \vdots \ g( oldsymbol{p}) \partial_n f( oldsymbol{p}) + f( oldsymbol{p})\partial_n g( oldsymbol{p})\end{bmatrix} = g( oldsymbol{p}) abla f( oldsymbol{p}) + f( oldsymbol{p}) abla g( oldsymbol{p})\]

Theorem: Quotient Rule with Gradients

Let \(f: \mathcal{D}_f \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) and \(g: \mathcal{D}_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be real scalar fields and let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} (\mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g)\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g\).

If \(f\) and \(g\) are both partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\) and \(g( oldsymbol{p}) e 0\), then \(f/g\) is also partially differentiable there and its gradient is given by the gradients of \(f\) and \(g\) as follows:

\[ abla(f/g)( oldsymbol{p}) = rac{g( oldsymbol{p}) abla f( oldsymbol{p}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) abla g( oldsymbol{p})}{g( oldsymbol{p})^2}\] Proof

Since \(f\) and \(g\) are both partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\) and \(g( oldsymbol{p}) e 0\), we know that their partial derivatives \(\partial_k f( oldsymbol{p})\) and \(\partial_k g( oldsymbol{p})\) exist for all \(k \in \{1, \dotsc, n\}\). We apply the quotient rule:

\[\partial_k (f/g)( oldsymbol{p}) = rac{(\partial_k f)( oldsymbol{p})g( oldsymbol{p}) - f( oldsymbol{p})(\partial_k g)( oldsymbol{p})}{g( oldsymbol{p})^2} = rac{g( oldsymbol{p}) \partial_k f( oldsymbol{p}) - f( oldsymbol{p})\partial_k g( oldsymbol{p})}{g( oldsymbol{p})^2}\]

Therefore, the gradient of \(f/g\) is the following:

\[ abla (f/g)( oldsymbol{p}) = egin{bmatrix} rac{g( oldsymbol{p}) \partial_1 f( oldsymbol{p}) - f( oldsymbol{p})\partial_1 g( oldsymbol{p})}{g( oldsymbol{p})^2} \ \vdots \ rac{g( oldsymbol{p}) \partial_n f( oldsymbol{p}) - f( oldsymbol{p})\partial_n g( oldsymbol{p})}{g( oldsymbol{p})^2}\end{bmatrix} = rac{g( oldsymbol{p}) abla f( oldsymbol{p}) - f( oldsymbol{p}) abla g( oldsymbol{p})}{g( oldsymbol{p})^2}\]

Theorem: Dot Product Rule

Let \(f: \mathcal{D}_f \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m o \mathbb{R}^n\) and \(g: \mathcal{D}_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m o \mathbb{R}^n\) be real vector functions and let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} (\mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g)\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}_f \cap \mathcal{D}_g\).

If \(f\) and \(g\) are partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\), then so is their dot product and its gradient is given by the transpositions of the Jacobian matrices of \(f\) and \(g\) as follows:

\[ abla (f\cdot g)( oldsymbol{p}) = J_f( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}}g( oldsymbol{p}) + J_g( oldsymbol{p})^{\mathsf{T}}f( oldsymbol{p})\] Proof

Theorem: Chain Rule with Real Functions

Let \(f: \mathcal{D}_f \subseteq \mathbb{R} o \mathbb{R}\) be a real function, let \(g: \mathcal{D}_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and with \(g(\mathcal{D}_g) \subseteq \mathcal{D}_f\) and let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}_g\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}_g\).

If \(g\) is partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\) and \(g( oldsymbol{p})\) is an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}_f\) and \(f\) is differentiable at \(g( oldsymbol{p})\), then the composition \(f\circ g\) is partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\) with the following gradient:

\[ abla (f \circ g)( oldsymbol{p}) = f'(g( oldsymbol{p})) abla g( oldsymbol{p})\] Example

Let \(f: \mathbb{R}_{\gt 0} o \mathbb{R}\) be a real function which is differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}_{\gt 0}\) and consider the real scalar field \(f(|| oldsymbol{x}||)\).

We have:

\[f(|| oldsymbol{x}||) = f\left(\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2} ight)\]

The partial derivatives of \(\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}\) are defined on \(\mathbb{R}^n\):

\[ egin{aligned}\partial_k\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2} = rac{2 x_k}{2\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}} = rac{x_k}{|| oldsymbol{x}||}\end{aligned}\]

The gradient of \(\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}\) at each \( oldsymbol{p} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ oldsymbol{0}\}\) is thus the following:

\[ abla \left(\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2} ight) ( oldsymbol{x}) = rac{1}{|| oldsymbol{x}||} oldsymbol{x}\]

Since \(f\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}_{\gt 0}\), the gradient of \(f(|| oldsymbol{x}||)\) at each \( oldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ oldsymbol{0}\}\) is the following:

\[ egin{aligned} abla f(|| oldsymbol{x}||) = rac{f'(|| oldsymbol{x}||)}{|| oldsymbol{x}||} oldsymbol{x}\end{aligned}\] Example: \(f( oldsymbol{x}) = \ln (|| oldsymbol{x}||)\)

From the above example, we know that \(f( oldsymbol{x}) = \ln (|| oldsymbol{x}||)\) is partially differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ oldsymbol{0}\}\) with the following gradient:

\[ abla \ln (|| oldsymbol{x}||) = rac{1}{|| oldsymbol{x}||} rac{1}{|| oldsymbol{x}||} oldsymbol{x} = rac{1}{|| oldsymbol{x}||^2} oldsymbol{x}\] Proof

Theorem: Chain Rule with Curves

Let \(f: \mathcal{D}_f \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field, and let \(g: \mathcal{D}_g \subseteq \mathbb{R} o \mathbb{R}^n\) be a parametric curve with \(g(\mathcal{D}_g) \subseteq \mathcal{D}_f\) and let \(t \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}_g\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}_g\).

If \(g\) is differentiable at \(t\) and \(g(t)\) is an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}_f\) and \(f\) is totally differentiable at \(g(t)\), then the composition \(f \circ g\) is differentiable at \(t\) and its derivative is the dot product of \(f\)'s gradient and \(g\)'s derivative:

\[(f\circ g)'(t) = abla f(g(t))\cdot g'(t)\] Example

Let \(g: [0,2\uppi] o \mathbb{R}^2\) be the curve defined as follows:

\[g(t) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} egin{bmatrix} \cos t \ \sin t \end{bmatrix}\]

Let \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 o \mathbb{R}\) be the real scalar field defined as follows:

\[f(x,y) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} x^2 + xy + y^2\]

We see that \(g\) is differentiable on \([0,2\uppi]\):

\[g'(t) = egin{bmatrix}-\sin t \ \cos t \end{bmatrix}\]

We also see that \(f\) is partially differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the following gradient:

\[ abla f (x,y) = egin{bmatrix}2x + y \ x + 2y\end{bmatrix}\]

We can also show that \(f\) is totally differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Therefore, \(f \circ g\) is differentiable on \([0, 2\uppi]\):

\[ egin{aligned}(f \circ g)'(t) & = abla f(g(t))^{\mathsf{T}}g'(t) \ & = egin{bmatrix}2 \cos t + \sin t & \cos t + 2\sin t\end{bmatrix} egin{bmatrix}-\sin t \ \cos t \end{bmatrix} \ & = (2 \cos t + \sin t)(-\sin t) + (\cos t + 2\sin t) \cos t \ & = \cos^2 t - \sin^2 t \ & = \cos (2t)\end{aligned}\] Proof

Since \(f\) is totally differentiable at \(g(t) \in \mathcal{D}_f\), we know that \(f(g(t) + oldsymbol{h}) - f(g(t)) - abla f(g(t))^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{h}\) is little o of \(|| oldsymbol{h}||\) for \( oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}\):

\[f(g(t) + oldsymbol{h}) - f(g(t)) - abla f(g(t))^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{h} = o(|| oldsymbol{h}||) \qquad ext{for} \qquad oldsymbol{h} o oldsymbol{0}\]

Theorem: Curl of Gradient

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field.

If \(f\) is twice totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{x} \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}\), then the curl of \(f\)'s gradient at \( oldsymbol{x}\) is zero:

\[\operatorname{curl} \operatorname{grad} f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{0}\] Proof

Let \(( abla f)_1, ( abla f)_2, ( abla f)_3\) be the component functions of \(f\)'s gradient:

\[ abla f ( oldsymbol{x}) = egin{bmatrix}( abla f)_1 ( oldsymbol{x}) \ ( abla f)_2( oldsymbol{x}) \ ( abla f)_3 ( oldsymbol{x})\end{bmatrix} = egin{bmatrix} \partial_1 f( oldsymbol{x}) \ \partial_2 f( oldsymbol{x}) \ \partial_3 f( oldsymbol{x}) \end{bmatrix}\]

The curl of \( abla f\) is the following:

\[ egin{aligned} abla imes abla f( oldsymbol{x}) & = egin{bmatrix} \partial_2 ( abla f)_3( oldsymbol{x}) - \partial_3 ( abla f)_2( oldsymbol{x}) \ \partial_3 ( abla f)_1( oldsymbol{x}) - \partial_1 ( abla f)_3( oldsymbol{x}) \ \partial_1 ( abla f)_2( oldsymbol{x}) - \partial_2 ( abla f)_1( oldsymbol{x}) \end{bmatrix} \ & = egin{bmatrix} \partial_2 \partial_3 f( oldsymbol{x}) - \partial_3 \partial_2 f( oldsymbol{x}) \ \partial_3 \partial_1 f( oldsymbol{x}) - \partial_1 \partial_3 f( oldsymbol{x}) \ \partial_1 \partial_2 f( oldsymbol{x}) - \partial_2 \partial_1 f( oldsymbol{x}) \end{bmatrix} \ & = egin{bmatrix} 0 \ 0 \ 0 \end{bmatrix} \ & = oldsymbol{0}\end{aligned}\]

Theorem: Mean Value Theorem via Gradient

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \( oldsymbol{a}, oldsymbol{b} \in \mathcal{D}\) such that \(L = \{ oldsymbol{a} + t( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a}) \mid t \in [0,1]\} \subseteq \mathcal{D}\).

If \(f\) is continuous on \(L\) and totally differentiable on \(\operatorname{int} L\), then there exists some \( oldsymbol{\xi} \in \operatorname{int} L\) such that \(f( oldsymbol{b}) - f( oldsymbol{a})\) is equal to the product of \(f\)'s gradient at \( oldsymbol{\xi}\) and \( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a}\):

\[f( oldsymbol{b}) - f( oldsymbol{a}) = abla f( oldsymbol{\xi}) \cdot ( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a})\] Example: \(f(x, y, z) = x^2 - 3y^2 + z\)

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathcal{D} o \mathbb{R}\) defined on \(\mathcal{D} = \{ oldsymbol{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid || oldsymbol{p}|| \le 1\}\) as follows:

\[f(x, y, z) = x^2 - 3y^2 + z\]

For all \( oldsymbol{a}, oldsymbol{b} \in \mathcal{D}\) and \(t \in [0,1]\), we have:

\[|| oldsymbol{a} + t( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a})|| = ||(1 - t) oldsymbol{a} + t oldsymbol{b}|| \le ||(1 - t) oldsymbol{a}|| + ||t oldsymbol{b}|| = |1 - t| || oldsymbol{a}|| + |t| || oldsymbol{b}||\]

Since \(t \in [0,1]\), we get:

\[|| oldsymbol{a} + t( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a})|| \le (1 - t) || oldsymbol{a}|| + t || oldsymbol{b}||\]

Since \( oldsymbol{a}, oldsymbol{b} \in \mathcal{D}\), we know that \(|| oldsymbol{a}|| \le 1\) and \(|| oldsymbol{b}|| \le 1\). Therefore:

\[|| oldsymbol{a} + t( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a})|| \le (1 - t) + t = 1\]

and so \(L = \{ oldsymbol{a} + t( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a}) \mid t \in [0, 1]\} \subseteq \mathcal{D}\).

We see that \(f\) is continuous on \(L\) and totally differentiable on \(\operatorname{int} L\). Therefore, there exists some \( oldsymbol{\xi} \in \operatorname{int} L\) such that

\[f( oldsymbol{b}) - f( oldsymbol{a}) = abla f( oldsymbol{\xi}) \cdot ( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a})\]

For the gradient of \(f\), we have

\[ abla f(x, y, z) = egin{bmatrix} 2 x \ -6 y \ 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

and so

\[|| abla f(x, y, z)|| = \sqrt{4x^2 + 36y^2 + 1} \le \sqrt{41}\]

for all \(x, y, z \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}\). Specifically, \(|| abla f( oldsymbol{\xi})|| \le \sqrt{41}\).

By applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to

\[ abla f( oldsymbol{\xi}) \cdot ( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a}),\]

we get the following:

\[| abla f( oldsymbol{\xi}) \cdot ( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a})| \le || abla f( oldsymbol{\xi})|| \, ||( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a})|| = \sqrt{41} || oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a}||\]

Since \( abla f( oldsymbol{\xi}) \cdot ( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a}) = f( oldsymbol{b}) - f( oldsymbol{a})\), we get:

\[|f( oldsymbol{b}) - f( oldsymbol{a})| \le \sqrt{41} || oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a}||\] Proof

From the mean value theorem via total differentials, we know that there exists some \( oldsymbol{\xi} \in \operatorname{int} L\) such that

\[f( oldsymbol{b}) - f( oldsymbol{a}) = \mathrm{d}f_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a})\]

Using the matrix representation of the total differential \(\mathrm{d}f_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}\), we get:

\[f( oldsymbol{b}) - f( oldsymbol{a}) = J_f( oldsymbol{\xi}) ( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a})\]

The Jacobian matrix \(J_f( oldsymbol{\xi})\) is just the transpose of the gradient \( abla f( oldsymbol{\xi})\):

\[f( oldsymbol{b}) - f( oldsymbol{a}) = abla f( oldsymbol{\xi})^{\mathsf{T}} ( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a})\] \[f( oldsymbol{b}) - f( oldsymbol{a}) = abla f( oldsymbol{\xi}) \cdot ( oldsymbol{b} - oldsymbol{a})\]

Theorem: Gradient in Polar Coordinates

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \(\mathcal{T}: (0, +\infty) imes (0, 2\uppi) o \mathbb{R}^2\) be the coordinate transformation from polar coordinates:

\[\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi) = egin{bmatrix} ho \cos \varphi \ ho \sin \varphi\end{bmatrix}\]

Let \( ilde{f} = f \circ \mathcal{T}\) be the polar coordinate representation of \(f\).

If \(f\) is totally differentiable at \(\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi)\), then its gradient at \(\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi)\) is expressed in the normalized local coordinate basis of polar coordinates using the partial derivatives of \( ilde{f}\) as follows:

\[( abla f)(\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi)) = \partial_{ ho} ilde{f}( ho, \varphi) oldsymbol{\hat{ ho}}( ho, \varphi) + rac{1}{ ho} \partial_{\varphi} ilde{f} ( ho, \varphi) oldsymbol{\hat{\varphi}}( ho, \varphi)\] Proof

Theorem: Gradient in Cylindrical Coordinates

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \(\mathcal{T}: (0,+\infty) imes (0,2\uppi) imes \mathbb{R} o \mathbb{R}^3\) be the coordinate transformation from cylindrical coordinates:

\[\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi, z) = egin{bmatrix} ho \cos \varphi \ ho \sin \varphi \ z\end{bmatrix}\]

Let \( ilde{f} = f \circ \mathcal{T}\) be the cylindrical coordinate representation of \(f\).

If \(f\) is totally differentiable at \(\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi, z)\), then its gradient at \(\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi, z)\) is expressed in the normalized local coordinate basis of cylindrical coordinates using the partial derivatives of \( ilde{f}\) as follows:

\[( abla f)(\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi, z)) = \partial_{ ho} ilde{f}( ho, \varphi, z) oldsymbol{\hat{ ho}}( ho, \varphi, z) + rac{1}{ ho} \partial_{\varphi} ilde{f}( ho, \varphi, z) oldsymbol{\hat{\varphi}}( ho, \varphi, z) + \partial_z ilde{f}( ho, \varphi, z) oldsymbol{\hat{z}}( ho, \varphi, z)\] Proof

Theorem: Gradient in Spherical Coordinates

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \(\mathcal{T}: (0,+\infty) imes (0,\uppi) imes (0,2\uppi) o \mathbb{R}^3\) be the coordinate transformation from spherical coordinates:

\[\mathcal{T}(r, heta, \varphi) = egin{bmatrix}r \sin heta \cos \varphi \ r \sin heta \sin \varphi \ r \cos heta\end{bmatrix}\]

Let \( ilde{f} = f \circ \mathcal{T}\) be the spherical coordinate representation of \(f\).

If \(f\) is totally differentiable at \(\mathcal{T}(r, heta, \varphi)\), then its gradient at \(\mathcal{T}(r, heta, \varphi)\) is expressed in the normalized local coordinate basis of spherical coordinates using \( ilde{f}\)'s partial derivatives as follows:

\[( abla f)(\mathcal{T}(r, heta, \varphi)) = \partial_r ilde{f}(r, heta, \varphi) oldsymbol{\hat{r}}(r, heta, \varphi) + rac{1}{r} \partial_{ heta} ilde{f}(r, heta, \varphi) oldsymbol{\hat{ heta}}(r, heta, \varphi) + rac{1}{r \sin heta} \partial_{\varphi} ilde{f}(r, heta, \varphi) oldsymbol{\hat{\varphi}}(r, heta, \varphi)\] Example: \(\ln (x^2 + y^2 +z^2)\)

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^3 \setminus oldsymbol{0} o \mathbb{R}\) defined as follows:

\[f(x, y, z) \overset{ ext{def}}{=}\ln (x^2 + y^2 + z^2)\]

In spherical coordinates, we have:

\[ egin{aligned} ilde{f}(r, heta, \varphi) & = (f \circ \mathcal{T})(r, heta, \varphi) \ & = \ln \left(r^2 \sin^2 heta \cos^2 \varphi + r^2 \sin^2 heta \sin^2 \varphi + r^2 \cos^2 heta ight) \ & = \ln (r^2 \sin^2 heta (\cos^2 \varphi + \sin^2 \varphi) + r^2 \cos^2 heta) \ & = \ln (r^2 \sin^2 heta + r^2 \cos^2 heta) \ & = \ln (r^2) \ & = 2 \ln r \end{aligned}\]

For its gradient, we have:

\[ egin{aligned} abla f(\mathcal{T}(r, heta, \varphi)) & = rac{\partial ilde{f}}{\partial r}(r, heta, \varphi) oldsymbol{\hat{r}}(r, heta, \varphi) + rac{1}{r} rac{\partial ilde{f}}{\partial heta}(r, heta, \varphi) oldsymbol{\hat{ heta}}(r, heta, \varphi) + rac{1}{r \sin heta} rac{\partial ilde{f}}{\partial \varphi}(r, heta, \varphi) oldsymbol{\hat{\varphi}}(r, heta, \varphi) \ & = rac{2}{r} \cdot oldsymbol{\hat{r}} + rac{1}{r} \cdot 0 \cdot oldsymbol{\hat{ heta}}(r, heta, \varphi) + rac{1}{r \sin heta} \cdot 0 \cdot oldsymbol{\hat{\varphi}}(r, heta, \varphi) \ & = rac{2}{r} oldsymbol{\hat{r}}(r, heta, \varphi) \ & = rac{2}{r} egin{bmatrix} \sin heta \cos \varphi \ \sin heta \sin \varphi \ \cos heta \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}\] Proof

docs.text:
Definition: Hessian Matrix

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field, let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}\) and suppose that \(f\) is twice partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\).

The Hessian matrix of \(f\) at \( oldsymbol{p}\) is \(n imes n\)-real matrix whose components are \(f\)'s second-order partial derivatives at \( oldsymbol{p}\):

\[ egin{bmatrix}\partial_1 \partial_1 f( oldsymbol{p}) & \cdots & \partial_1\partial_n f( oldsymbol{p}) \ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ \partial_n \partial_1 f( oldsymbol{p}) & \cdots & \partial_n\partial_n f( oldsymbol{p})\end{bmatrix}\]

Tip: Hessian Matrix and Gradients

The columns of the Hessian matrix are just the gradients of \(f\)'s partial derivatives:

\[H_f( oldsymbol{p}) = egin{bmatrix}\vert & \vert & \vert \ abla(\partial_1 f)( oldsymbol{p}) & \cdots & abla(\partial_n f)( oldsymbol{p}) \ \vert & \vert & \vert \end{bmatrix}\]

Notation

\[H_f( oldsymbol{p})\] Example: \(f(x, y) = x^2 y^3 + x\)

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 o \mathbb{R}\) defined as follows:

\[f\left(x, y ight) = x^2 y^3 + x\]

It is twice partially differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\):

\[\partial_x f (x, y) = 2x y^3 + 1 \qquad \partial_x \partial_x f(x,y) = 2y^3 \qquad \partial_{y} \partial_x f(x,y) = 6x y^2\] \[\partial_y f (x, y) = 3 x^2 y^2 \qquad \partial_x \partial_y f(x,y) = 6x y^2 \qquad \partial_y \partial_y f(x,y) = 6 x^2 y\]

Its Hessian matrix is thus the following for all \( egin{bmatrix}x & y\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}} \in \mathbb{R}^2\):

\[H_f(x,y) = egin{bmatrix} \partial_x \partial_x f(x,y) & \partial_x \partial_y f(x,y) \ \partial_y \partial_x f(x,y) & \partial_y \partial_y f(x,y) \end{bmatrix} = egin{bmatrix} 2y^3 & 6x y^2 \ 6x y^2 & 6 x^2 y\end{bmatrix}\] Example: \(f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x}\)

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{a}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{x}\]

for some fixed real vector \( oldsymbol{a} = egin{bmatrix} a^1 & \cdots & a^n \end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}}\in \mathbb{R}^n\).

Its Hessian matrix is zero everywhere:

\[H_f( oldsymbol{p}) = oldsymbol{0}\] Example: \(f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x}\)

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) defined as

\[f( oldsymbol{x}) = oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}} oldsymbol{A} oldsymbol{x}\]

for some real matrix \( oldsymbol{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n imes n}\).

Its Hessian matrix is the following:

\[H_f( oldsymbol{p}) = oldsymbol{A} + oldsymbol{A}^{\mathsf{T}}\] Example: \(f( oldsymbol{x}) = || oldsymbol{x}||\)

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) defined as follows:

\[f( oldsymbol{x}) = || oldsymbol{x}||\]

It is totally differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ oldsymbol{0}\}\) with the following partial derivatives:

\[\partial_{i}f( oldsymbol{x}) = rac{x_i}{|| oldsymbol{x}||}\]

We thus have:

\[\partial_{i}\partial_{i}f( oldsymbol{x}) = rac{|| oldsymbol{x}|| - x_i rac{x_i}{|| oldsymbol{x}||}}{|| oldsymbol{x}||^2} = rac{1}{|| oldsymbol{x}||} - rac{x_i^2}{|| oldsymbol{x}||^3}\] \[\partial_{i}\partial_{j} f( oldsymbol{x}) = - rac{x_i x_j}{|| oldsymbol{x}||^3} \qquad i e j\]

For its Hessian matrix, we have:

\[H_f( oldsymbol{x}) = rac{1}{|| oldsymbol{x}||}I_n - rac{1}{|| oldsymbol{x}||^3} oldsymbol{x} oldsymbol{x}^{\mathsf{T}}\]

Theorem: Symmetry of the Hessian Matrix

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}\).

If \(f\) is twice totally differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\), then its Hessian matrix there is symmetric.

docs.text:
Definition: Laplacian (Real Scalar Fields)

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field, let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}\) be an interior point of \(\mathcal{D}_f\), suppose that \(f\) is partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\) and suppose that each partial derivative \(\partial_k f\) is itself partially differentiable at \( oldsymbol{p}\) with respect to the \(k\)-th variable.

The Laplacian of \(f\) at \( oldsymbol{p}\) is defined as follows:

\[\sum_{k = 1}^n \partial_k \partial_k f( oldsymbol{p})\]

Notation

\[ abla^2 f ( oldsymbol{p}) \qquad \Delta f( oldsymbol{p})\] Example: \(f(x,y) = \sin(\uppi x)\sin (\uppi y)\)

Consider the real scalar field \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 o \mathbb{R}\) defined as follows:

\[f(x, y) \overset{ ext{def}}{=} \sin(\uppi x)\sin (\uppi y)\]

We see that \(f\) is partially differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\):

\[\partial_x f(x,y) = \uppi \cos (\uppi x) \sin(\uppi y) \qquad \partial_y f(x,y) = \uppi \sin (\uppi x) \cos (\uppi y)\]

Similarly, we see that \(\partial_x f\) is partially differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with respect to \(x\):

\[\partial_x \partial_x f(x,y) = - \uppi^2 \sin(\uppi x)\sin (\uppi y)\]

By the same token, \(\partial_y f\) is partially differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with respect to \(y\):

\[\partial_y \partial_y f(x,y) = - \uppi^2 \sin(\uppi x)\sin (\uppi y)\]

Therefore, the Laplacian of \(f\) exists at each \( egin{bmatrix}x & y\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}} \in \mathbb{R}^2\):

\[ egin{aligned} abla^2 f (x,y) & = \partial_x \partial_x f(x,y) + \partial_y \partial_y f(x,y) \ & = - \uppi^2 \sin(\uppi x)\sin (\uppi y) - \uppi^2 \sin(\uppi x)\sin (\uppi y) \ & = -2 \uppi^2 \sin(\uppi x)\sin (\uppi y)\end{aligned}\]

Theorem: Laplacian = Divergence of Gradient

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field, let \( oldsymbol{p} \in \operatorname{int} \mathcal{D}\) be an interior point of \(f\).

If TODO, then the Laplacian of \(f\) at \( oldsymbol{p}\) is the divergence of \(f\)'s gradient at \( oldsymbol{p}\):

\[ abla^2 f ( oldsymbol{p}) = \operatorname{div} \operatorname{grad} f( oldsymbol{p})\] Proof

Theorem: Laplacian from Polar Coordinate Representation

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 o \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field and let \(\mathcal{T}: (0, +\infty) imes (0, 2\uppi) o \mathbb{R}^2\) be the coordinate transformation from polar coordinates:

\[\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi) = egin{bmatrix} ho \cos \varphi \ ho \sin \varphi\end{bmatrix}\]

Let \( ilde{f} = f \circ \mathcal{T}\) be the polar coordinate representation of \(f\).

If \(f\) is twice totally differentiable at \(\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi)\), then its Laplacian at \(\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi)\) is expressed using partial derivatives of \( ilde{f}\) as follows:

\[( abla^2 f) (\mathcal{T}( ho, \varphi)) = (\partial_{ ho} (\partial_{ ho} ilde{f}))( ho, \varphi) + rac{1}{ ho} \partial_{ ho} ilde{f}( ho, \varphi) + rac{1}{ ho^2} (\partial_{\varphi} (\partial_{\varphi} ilde{f}))( ho, \varphi)\] Proof

docs.text:
Definition: Partial Antidifferentiability

Let \(f: \mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) be a real scalar field.

We say that \(f\) is partially antidifferentiable on an open set \(U \subseteq \mathcal{D}\) with respect to the \(k\)-th variable if there exists a real scalar field \(F: U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) whose partial derivative w.r.t. the \(k\)-variable is \(f\):

\[\partial_k F = f\]

We call \(F\) a partial antiderivative of \(f\) with respect to the \(k\)-th variable.

Notation

If the components of the input are labelled \(x_1, \dotsc, x_n\), i.e. \(f(x_1, \dotsc, x_n)\), then the set of all partial antiderivatives of \(f\) on \(U\) w.r.t. the \(k\)-th variable is denoted as follows:

\[\int f(x_1, \dotsc, x_n) \,\mathrm{d}x_k\]
